articles.title: TSE vai limitar decisão de André Mendonça ao que é de fato fake news contra Flávio Bolsonaro | G1
articles.body:
O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) deve limitar o alcance da decisão do ministro André Mendonça às publicações que associam o candidato à Presidência Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) a uma iniciativa para retirar de Nossa Senhora Aparecida o título de padroeira do Brasil.

Segundo apurou o blog , vários ministros devem apresentar votos para restringir a decisão de Mendonça, considerada ampla demais.

A proposta que tende a prevalecer é preservar manifestações protegidas pela liberdade de expressão e pela liberdade religiosa, além de críticas jornalísticas e sátiras, desde que não atribuam a Flávio Bolsonaro a autoria , o apoio ou a articulação de uma proposta para retirar o título da santa.

A avaliação interna é que Mendonça acertou ao determinar a remoção da informação que fazem associação a Flávio Bolsonaro, mas foi longe demais ao alcançar publicações que não citavam o candidato do PL e tratavam do debate religioso envolvendo católicos e evangélicos.

No domingo (27), o ministro Flávio Dino, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), derrubou a ordem em relação a essas publicações, argumentando que era necessário proteger a liberdade de expressão.

Na segunda (28), o ministro Luiz Fux suspendeu a decisão de Dino e restabeleceu a determinação de Mendonça até que o caso fosse analisado de forma colegiada.

Ao defender sua posição, Mendonça também procurou deixar claro que sua decisão não teve como objetivo restringir a liberdade de expressão ou a liberdade religiosa.

O posicionamento dialoga diretamente com os argumentos usados por Dino ao derrubar a ordem do TSE.

Nos bastidores, a decisão de Nunes Marques de levar o caso ao plenário do TSE também ajuda a reduzir a tensão institucional com o Supremo.

O presidente do STF, Edson Fachin, conversou com Kassio Nunes Marques , e os dois entenderam que o melhor caminho seria deixar a questão ser resolvida pelo plenário da Justiça Eleitoral.

Com isso, Fachin decidiu não levar o tema ao plenário do Supremo nesta quarta, abrindo espaço para uma solução dentro do TSE.

Nunes Marques poderia ter evitado que a crise entre TSE e STF se agravasse se tivesse submetido a decisão de Mendonça ao plenário da Corte Eleitoral ainda na semana passada. Aliados chegaram a defender esse caminho imediatamente após a ordem de retirada das publicações.

Como isso não ocorreu, abriu-se espaço para a intervenção de Dino no caso e para uma disputa no Supremo sobre os limites da atuação individual de ministros diante de uma decisão da Justiça Eleitoral.

articles.title: Claudia Leitte é confirmada para abrir Micareta de Feira 2026 | G1
articles.standfirst: Festa gratuita acontece entre 19 e 22 de novembro. Além de Claudia Leitte, artistas como Léo Santana e Carlinhos Brown também foram confirmados.
articles.summary: Festa gratuita acontece entre 19 e 22 de novembro. Além de Claudia Leitte, artistas como Léo Santana e Carlinhos Brown também foram confirmados.
articles.body:
Claudia Leitte desfila no circuito Dodô (Barra-Ondina) com o bloco "Largadinho" — Foto: Dodo Villar/Divulgação

A cantora Claudia Leitte foi confirmada como atração do primeiro dia da Micareta de Feira 2026. Ela se apresenta em 19 de novembro, na Avenida Presidente Dutra, em Feira de Santana , segunda maior cidade da Bahia.

O anúncio foi feito pelo prefeito José Ronaldo de Carvalho (União Brasil), em um vídeo publicado nas redes sociais na terça-feira (29). Claudia Leitte também comemorou a participação e afirmou que está chegando para a festa.

A Micareta será realizada entre 19 e 22 de novembro. Esta será a primeira vez que o evento acontecerá no segundo semestre. Em 2025, a festa foi realizada entre 1º e 4 de maio.

Com uma carreira marcada pelo axé e por apresentações em trios elétricos, Claudia Leitte retorna à tradicional festa. No último ano, ela se emocionou ao puxar trio elétrico onde morou e estreou há 30 anos.

Além de Claudia Leitte, a programação já reúne artistas de diferentes estilos . Entre os nomes confirmados estão Léo Santana, Pedro Sampaio, Pablo, Xanddy Harmonia, Olodum, Carlinhos Brown, Edson Gomes, Tomate, Timbalada, Alinne Rosa, Michele Andrade e Milsinho, vocalista da banda Toque Dez.

A programação completa ainda será divulgada pela prefeitura.

A mudança da Micareta de Feira para o segundo semestre foi anunciada pela Prefeitura de Feira de Santana em outubro de 2025. Segundo o município, a alteração busca evitar impactos provocados pelas chuvas e ampliar o período disponível para planejamento e organização do evento.

Em 2025, mais de 1 milhão de pessoas participaram da festa. A programação contou com atrações como BaianaSystem e Rachel Reis na Praça da Matriz, além do tradicional arrastão.

articles.title: Fachin pediu a Nunes Marques para resolver crise do caso Nossa Senhora primeiro no TSE | G1
articles.standfirst: Nos bastidores, presidentes do STF e TSE conversaram e entedimento de Fachin é de que só após a Justiça Eleitoral julgar o tema que vai dcidir se caso será pautado no Supremo e quando.
articles.summary: Nos bastidores, presidentes do STF e TSE conversaram e entedimento de Fachin é de que só após a Justiça Eleitoral julgar o tema que vai dcidir se caso será pautado no Supremo e quando.
articles.body:
O agendamento da sessão do plenário virtual do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) que vai julgar o caso de Nossa Senhora Aparecida, nesta quarta-feira (30) , passou por uma conversa de bastidor e um acordo entre o presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), Edson Fachin , e o presidente da Justiça Eleitoral, Kassio Nunes Marques.

O blog apurou que Fachin pediu que o TSE decidisse primeiro sobre o caso de Aparecida para, só depois, o Supremo avaliar a questão — inclusive se ela ainda será uma questão.

Nessa conversa, Fachin pediu para, primeiramente, ver a posição do colegiado do TSE sobre a decisão e, só depois, avaliar se vai ser necessário o Supremo atuar, a partir da decisão que sair do plenário virtual.

Pode haver pedido de vista no STF após a decisão colegiada do TSE. No entanto, uma decisão tomada no plenário da Justiça Eleitoral derruba as decisões liminares decretadas no Supremo.

Nesta quarta (30), o TSE analisa a decisão do ministro André Mendonça que removeu as publicações que associavam o candidato Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) a um suposto movimento de retirada de Nossa Senhora Aparecida do posto de padroeira do Brasil.

Na segunda-feira (28), o ministro Luiz Fux, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) suspendeu a decisão do ministro Flávio Dino que havia derrubado a ordem do ministro Mendonça.

Na prática, isso significa que os posts devem permanecer fora do ar.

Ministro Edson Fachin do STF — Foto: Rosinei Coutinho/STF

O julgamento começou no TSE, com a decisão de Mendonça. Um recurso levou o caso ao ministro Flávio Dino, do STF, que suspendeu a decisão e levou a questão ao Supremo.

A defesa do candidato Flávio Bolsonaro entrou com uma nova ação enviada a Luiz Fux, que suspendeu a decisão de Dino e retomou os efeitos da proibição decretada por Mendonça.

Após Flávio Bolsonaro recorrer da derrubada da decisão de Mendonça, Dino já havia enviado a decisão dele para aprovação no plenário.

O presidente do STF, ministro Edson Fachin, chegou a sinalizar que pautaria o assunto nesta quarta-feira (30), o que não chegou a ser confirmado.

articles.title: Duelo entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro define jogo de poder no STF | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministros ouvidos pelo blog entendem que vitória de Lula tende a fortalecer grupo ligado a Moraes. Já a eleição de Flávio Bolsonaro pode ampliar o poder do grupo de Kassio Nunes Marques e André Mendonça, indicados pelo ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro.
articles.summary: A disputa entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro definirá o poder no STF, fortalecendo o grupo de Alexandre de Moraes ou os ministros indicados por Jair Bolsonaro.
articles.body:
A disputa entre Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) escancara uma outra guerra que está sendo travada nesta eleição: a disputa pelo futuro dos grupos de poder dentro do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ).

De acordo com ministros do STF ouvidos pelo blog , o que fica claro é que o resultado das urnas será lido também como uma medição de forças dentro dos tribunais — sobre quem sai fortalecido, quem perde espaço e quem terá mais poder no pós-eleição.

É por isso que a guerra entre TSE e Supremo virou protagonista desta reta final. O que está em jogo não é apenas qual grupo político ganha ou perde nas urnas, nem as preferências de cada ministro. Está em jogo também quem termina essa eleição de pé dentro dos tribunais.

De um lado, o grupo de Alexandre de Moraes. Do outro, o grupo de Kassio Nunes Marques e André Mendonça. Uma guerra interna do Supremo que transbordou para o TSE.

A avaliação de ministros ouvidos pelo blog é a seguinte: uma vitória de Lula tende a fortalecer o grupo de Moraes e ampliar seu poder para tentar esvaziar o grupo de Kassio e Mendonça. Uma vitória de Flávio Bolsonaro, na leitura desses ministros, produziria o movimento inverso: fortaleceria Kassio e Mendonça e aumentaria a pressão sobre o grupo de Moraes e Flávio Dino — inclusive dando novo combustível político a movimentos por impeachment.

Ministros dizem ao blog que, independentemente do resultado da eleição, a ofensiva deve continuar na semana que vem. O grupo de Moraes pretende continuar pressionando Kassio e André Mendonça e fala em novas revelações sobre eventuais irregularidades envolvendo o grupo adversário.

É dentro desse contexto que precisa ser lida também a ofensiva para retirar Kassio e André da comissão que discute propaganda no TSE. É uma medição de forças por espaço, comando e poder dentro dos tribunais.

Então há duas disputas acontecendo simultaneamente: Lula e Flávio disputam nas urnas o comando do país; dentro dos tribunais, grupos de ministros olham para esse mesmo resultado pensando no próprio futuro e na correlação de forças do pós-eleição.

A eleição acaba nas urnas. A guerra no Supremo continua depois delas.

articles.title: Lula informa que não vai participar do debate da Globo | G1
articles.standfirst: Estão confirmados os candidatos Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), Augusto Cury (Avante) e Romeu Zema (Novo).
articles.summary: Estão confirmados os candidatos Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), Augusto Cury (Avante) e Romeu Zema (Novo).
articles.body:
A assessoria do presidente Lula, candidato à reeleição pelo PT, informou à Globo nesta quarta-feira (30) que ele não participará do debate que será realizado pela emissora, nesta quinta-feira (1º) à noite.

Estão confirmados no debate os candidatos Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), Augusto Cury (Avante) e Romeu Zema (Novo).

Mediado pelo jornalista César Tralli, o encontro será transmitido ao vivo pela TV Globo direto dos Estúdios Globo, no Rio de Janeiro, e também poderá ser visto simultaneamente no g1 e na GloboNews.

O debate será logo após o Jornal Nacional, com início previsto para as 21h30. Pela primeira vez, o programa ocupará a faixa da novela das 21h, "Quem Ama Cuida".

O programa terá quatro blocos de perguntas e respostas, além das considerações finais. Dois blocos são de temas determinados e dois, de tema livre.

A dinâmica dos candidatos acontece ao redor de um mapa do Brasil posicionado no centro do cenário.

Por meio do mapa, o debate abordará as regiões do Brasil e temas específicos como a preservação da Amazônia; segurança nas fronteiras e combate ao crime organizado; e desafios para melhorar a infraestrutura para as exportações brasileiras.

Além disso, os candidatos poderão escolher entre temas predefinidos no telão para fazer as suas perguntas.

O candidato que faz a pergunta terá dois minutos para dividir entre a formulação da questão e a réplica. O candidato que responde terá três minutos para dividir entre resposta e tréplica.

Decisão de Nunes Marques sobre candidatos do Novo

Na terça-feira (29), o ministro Nunes Marques, presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), concedeu uma decisão liminar (provisória) requerida pelo Partido Novo , alterando entendimento anterior do TSE que define os critérios de participação de partidos em debates eleitorais em emissoras de rádio e TV.

A decisão garantiu a participação dos candidatos do Partido Novo nos debates das eleições de 2026 em todas as emissoras de rádio e TV a partir de terça.

O ministro determinou que os candidatos do Novo ao governo do Distrito Federal (DF), Kiko Caputo, e do Rio de Janeiro (RJ), André Marinho, participassem dos debates realizados pela Globo na noite de terça.

A decisão também beneficia o candidato a presidente pelo Novo, Romeu Zema.

articles.title: Temporal causa estragos em Euclides da Cunha Paulista; veja a previsão | G1
articles.standfirst: Ocorrências foram registradas nesta terça-feira (29), com quedas de árvores e postes e avanço de erosão que levou à interdição preventiva de uma casa. Nesta quarta-feira (30), há previsão de pancadas de chuva, rajadas de vento e possibilidade de granizo.
articles.summary: Uma forte chuva acompanhada de rajadas de vento provocou quedas de árvores e postes, além de danos em diferentes pontos de Euclides da Cunha Paulista (SP), nesta terça-feira (29).
articles.body:
Estragos foram registrados em Euclides da Cunha Paulista devido à chuva — Foto: Defesa Civil

Uma forte chuva acompanhada de rajadas de vento provocou quedas de árvores e postes, além de danos em diferentes pontos de Euclides da Cunha Paulista (SP), por volta das 15h desta terça-feira (29).

Conforme a Defesa Civil Municipal, as ocorrências foram registradas em diversas vias. Na Rua Francisco Maturano Moreno, a força da água provocou o avanço da erosão, levando à interdição preventiva de uma residência vizinha.

Todas as vias foram liberadas e o fornecimento de energia foi restabelecido. Não houve registro de feridos ou desabrigados.

Mais cedo, entre a noite de segunda-feira (28) e a manhã desta terça-feira (29), rajadas de vento de até 72,2 km/h foram registradas em Presidente Prudente (SP) e provocaram quedas de árvores em algumas localidades do município. Ninguém se feriu.

Além disso, um voo da Azul que partiu do Aeroporto Internacional de Viracopos, com destino a Presidente Prudente , foi prejudicado durante a madrugada. Segundo a Aeroportos Paulistas (ASP), a aeronave precisou voltar ao aeroporto de origem em razão das condições meteorológicas.

Nesta quarta-feira (30), grande parte do estado de São Paulo amanheceu com bastante nebulosidade, temperaturas amenas e registro de chuvas isoladas, conforme a Defesa Civil Estadual.

Ao longo do dia, o território paulista será influenciado pela atuação de um cavado meteorológico e pela aproximação de uma frente fria, favorecendo o aumento da instabilidade, principalmente nas regiões que fazem divisa com o Paraná e na faixa leste do estado .

Diante desse cenário, há possibilidade de pancadas de chuva em pontos isolados de todo o estado de SP, sobretudo a partir da tarde . As chuvas poderão vir acompanhadas de descargas elétricas, rajadas de vento, que pontualmente podem superar os 70 km/h, e eventual queda de granizo.

Várias regiões do estado de SP podem registrar chuva nesta quarta-feira (30) — Foto: Defesa Civil de SP/Divulgação

Apesar do aumento da instabilidade, o calor e a sensação de tempo abafado devem predominar ao longo do dia.

No interior paulista, o sol aparecerá entre poucas nuvens, enquanto nas demais regiões a nebulosidade será mais persistente. As temperaturas máximas das regionais da faixa leste do estado devem variar entre 26°C e 32°C, enquanto nas demais regionais os termômetros poderão alcançar valores entre 33°C e 35°C.

articles.title: Voto útil já começou — e beneficia quem lidera em cada estado | G1
articles.standfirst: Análise de dados das pesquisas Quaest de setembro mostra que há um movimento de esvaziamento da terceira via e de migração para as candidaturas de Lula e de Flávio Bolsonaro.
articles.summary: O voto útil já começou a desidratar a terceira via e fortalecer Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro nos estados, segundo análise de dados da pesquisa Quaest.
articles.body:
Urnas eletrônicas em Alagoas prontas para eleições 2026 - 20.09.2026 — Foto: Luiz Roberto/TSE

Em 1997, o cientista político Gary Cox publicou "Making Votes Count", o livro que se tornou a referência sobre como as regras eleitorais moldam o comportamento do eleitor. A ideia central é simples: o voto útil não é um ato de traição às convicções, mas um cálculo. O eleitor abandona o candidato de sua preferência quando percebe que ele não tem chance de vencer e que insistir nele pode facilitar a vitória justamente daquele que mais rejeita.

Para esse cálculo acontecer, Cox mostra que três condições precisam estar presentes: o eleitor se importa com o resultado (não vota apenas para expressar uma identidade), sabe quem é viável e quem não é, e essa informação é compartilhada por todos — o que, nas democracias modernas, é o papel das pesquisas. Quando os três ingredientes se combinam, a disputa converge para os dois nomes com chances reais, e os demais encolhem. Cox chama isso de "deserção estratégica".

As últimas três rodadas da Quaest em São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, Pernambuco e Distrito Federal mostram esse mecanismo em funcionamento. Somei, em cada estado, as intenções de voto de Augusto Cury (Avante), Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), Romeu Zema (Novo) e Renan Santos (Missão) — os quatro nomes que disputam o espaço fora da polarização — e comparei com a evolução da vantagem de quem lidera o primeiro turno nas três últimas rodadas (8, 23 e 29 de setembro). O padrão é consistente: a terceira via murcha e o voto migra para o candidato que já estava na frente naquele território.

Quaest para Globo, rodadas de 8, 23 e 29 de setembro de 2026, PE, MG, RJ, SP e DF — Foto: Reprodução

Em quatro dos cinco estados, a queda da terceira via se converte em vantagem maior para quem já liderava; em Minas, os dois crescem igualmente e a dianteira do presidente Lula (PT) fica em 4 pontos.

Em Pernambuco, o bloco de candidatos fora da polarização foi de 10% em 8 de setembro para 6% agora. No mesmo período, Lula subiu de 51% para 58%, enquanto Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) oscilou de 21% para 20%. A vantagem do presidente, que era de 30 pontos, foi a 38. O eleitor pernambucano que experimentou Cury em setembro voltou para seu voto de origem.

No Rio de Janeiro, o movimento é o espelho. A terceira via foi de 12% para 8%; Flávio Bolsonaro saiu de 34% para 38% e Lula oscilou de 32% para 31%. A vantagem do senador, que era de 2 pontos, chegou a 7. Em São Paulo, o bloco foi de 15% para 13%, Flávio subiu cinco pontos (de 31% para 36%) e Lula ficou onde estava, em 30%. A dianteira bolsonarista passou de 1 para 6 pontos.

No Distrito Federal está o caso mais claro. Caiado, que chegou a ter 13% na capital federal, hoje tem 8%, e o conjunto da terceira via caiu de 24% para 16%. Flávio foi de 31% para 38% e abriu 6 pontos sobre Lula, que subiu menos.

Minas Gerais é a exceção que confirma a lógica de Cox. A terceira via desinflou de 19% para 14% depois do pico de Augusto Cury, mas Lula e Flávio cresceram os mesmos quatro pontos, e a vantagem do presidente, de 4 pontos, apenas se consolidou. Minas segue sendo o estado mais equilibrado dos cinco — e, por isso, aquele em que o voto útil ainda não decidiu o primeiro turno. Sem ter uma clareza sobre quem lidera, o voto útil não produz vantagem para nenhum dos lados.

O que une os cinco estados não é a direção do movimento, e sim sua lógica. O voto útil não tem lado: ele fortalece quem já lidera onde o eleitor percebe que a disputa está definida. No Nordeste, isso amplia Lula. No Rio, em São Paulo e em Brasília, amplia Flávio Bolsonaro. A terceira via, que em setembro chegou a somar quase um quarto dos votos no Distrito Federal e um quinto em Minas, está sendo drenada pelas duas pontas da polarização, exatamente como Cox previu há quase trinta anos.

Para os candidatos de fora da polarização, a lição é dura. Cox mostra que a deserção estratégica se acelera à medida que a eleição se aproxima e as pesquisas tornam a hierarquia dos candidatos consenso público. Faltando pouco para o primeiro turno, cada nova rodada de pesquisa que confirma a distância entre os dois líderes e os demais funciona como um sinal para o eleitor: insistir no preferido tem custo. E o eleitor brasileiro, como mostram os números, está fazendo a conta.

articles.title: Crise institucional no STF: perfil político de ministros amplia divisões | G1
articles.standfirst: A presença de ministros com trajetória política no Supremo tem ampliado divisões internas e levado disputas do STF para o TSE.
articles.summary: A crise institucional no STF se intensifica com a influência de perfis políticos, gerando novos conflitos de competência e divisões internas com o TSE.
articles.body:
A crise envolvendo ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) e do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) expôs uma disputa entre diferentes grupos dentro do Judiciário sobre a atuação dos integrantes das duas cortes. Parte dos ministros do STF questiona decisões tomadas no TSE e defende que determinadas questões sejam submetidas ao Supremo.

O TSE é composto por sete ministros, sendo três deles integrantes do STF: Kassio Nunes Marques , André Mendonça e Dias Toffoli .

Em geral, as decisões do TSE não podem ser levadas a outro tribunal. Há, porém, uma exceção: quando uma decisão é considerada contrária à Constituição, a questão pode ser levada ao STF para análise.

Nesse cenário, ganha relevância o perfil dos atuais integrantes do STF. A Corte reúne hoje mais ministros com passagem pela política, como Flávio Dino , Alexandre de Moraes e André Mendonça. Isso teria contribuído para ampliar a formação de grupos com posições distintas dentro dos tribunais superiores.

A origem da tensão é associada ainda a desdobramentos do caso Master. Episódios envolvendo ministros foram sendo tratados sem uma solução definitiva e ganharam dimensão ao longo das investigações da Polícia Federal e de discussões posteriores no Supremo.

O resultado é uma disputa que já ultrapassa casos específicos e envolve diferentes visões sobre o funcionamento do STF e do TSE.

articles.title: SEN RAND PAUL: Our budget deficit is out of control. Congress must pass my Six Penny Plan
articles.summary: The U.S. national debt has surpassed $40 trillion, and my Six Penny Plan aims to balance the budget within five years by cutting six pennies per dollar.
articles.body: In 2011, our national debt was about $15 trillion, and the U.S. Treasury spent over $450 billion on interest. Washington was printing money it didn’t have, buying its way out of yet another financial crisis and sending brand-new, taxpayer-funded subsidies to health insurance companies through Obamacare. It was clear then that this massive level of spending was not sustainable. It was in this moment of explosive deficit spending that a new generation of conservative leaders — myself included — rode into Congress on a mandate from the American people to restore fiscal sanity and financial freedom. I left my medical practice to stand for public office because I would not let our children and grandchildren be bankrupted by reckless politicians. The fight for fiscal responsibility continues, and I plan to force a vote on my latest balanced budget proposal — the Six Penny Plan — later this year. GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US' But I regret to inform you that Congress has completely lost the plot. Under the Six Penny Plan, Congress needs to find a six-percentage-point cut each year for five years. After that, once the budget is balanced, spending can increase based on the additional revenue from economic growth. The national debt has now surpassed $40 trillion. Congress now spends over $1 trillion on interest every year. Congress spends more on interest than on national defense. This enormous debt is contributing to rising interest rates and inflation, hurting every American. It’s a blinking red warning light — just as bright and red as the ink on our budget documents. Congress’ answer to this growing fiscal bomb? More of the same. Congress passed a continuing resolution earlier this summer to extend the status quo and will debate another extension before the end of this year. The good news is that it doesn’t have to be this way. When Congress takes up government funding later this year, it can pass my Six Penny Plan, which will balance the budget within five years. $50 TRILLION IN DEBT IS NOT A DISTANT THREAT. AMERICA IS SPEEDING TOWARDS IT No one can say he or she supports a balanced budget while voting against the only balanced budget that came up for a vote. No more empty promises. No more excuses. No more games. The Six Penny Plan doesn’t prescribe any particular program or budget category to be cut — it even specifically exempts Social Security from cuts. The Six Penny Plan simply sets a maximum spending level. What Congress wants to do within that maximum is up for debate. This budget reflects the basic questions of priorities many Americans have confronted at different points in their lives, whether because of unexpected expenses or a loss of income: Which expenses can Congress keep, and which can Congress cut? Under the Six Penny Plan, Congress needs to find a 6% cut each year for five years. After that, once the budget is balanced, spending can increase based on the additional revenue from economic growth. WASHINGTON IS DRIVING AMERICA TOWARD A DEBT CRISIS WE CAN'T IGNORE ANY LONGER Interestingly, when I first proposed what became the Penny Plan in 2018, Congress would not have had to find any cuts, but merely work within a spending freeze for five years. Its inaction then is only making the job harder now. In subsequent years, it became the Penny Plan when it required a 1% cut, then it became the "Pennies Plan," and today it is the Six Penny Plan because it requires us to find six pennies out of every dollar. CONGRESS SPENDS $7 TRILLION. HERE’S HOW THAT MATH WORKS OUT IF YOU THINK OF JUST $100 Kicking the can down the road has been standard procedure in Congress for too long. Lawmakers have treated the debt like someone else’s problem, to be dealt with some other day in the future. Well, the future has arrived. Every year that Congress does nothing only adds fuel to the debt bomb and increases the risk of a bigger explosion down the road. It’s also time to call inaction on the debt what it is: a vote to increase the hidden inflation tax on everyone; a willful decision to let inflation wreak havoc on our cost of living. Inaction is unacceptable. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The Six Penny Plan is the answer. The good news is that, when it was voted on in 2024 and 2025, the Six Penny Plan was supported by a majority of Senate Republicans. Because a budget resolution needs only a majority vote to pass, rather than a supermajority, Senate Republicans have the numbers to pass the Six Penny Plan. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In other words, this is the moment. Support for the Six Penny Plan has been building, and there should be enough votes. Let’s show that conservatives mean what we say and can follow through on our promises to balance the budget. Let’s pass the Six Penny Plan. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM SEN RAND PAUL

articles.title: Maine Dem Sen candidate's 'working class' cred shredded by both parties when internet sees latest 'cringey' ad
articles.summary: Troy Jackson's boba tea ad mocking Susan Collins and Elon Musk has been viewed over 2 million times, drawing sharp bipartisan ridicule on X.
articles.body: Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger who has touted his working-class bonafides on the campaign trail, is facing backlash from both sides of the aisle over a viral ad that critics are labeling as tone-deaf pandering. "If Republicans spend $46 million on these TV ads, who’s gunna be convinced by that?" Jackson is asked in the ad as he sips a boba tea. Jackson then looks around and smiles before saying "the 1%ers" as a photo of his opponent, Sen. Susan Collins, and Tesla CEO Elon Musk are shown on the screen. The ad’s caption reads "sips boba tea" alongside a boba and wide-eyed emoji. SUSAN COLLINS TEARS INTO BRIBERY ALLEGATIONS AS NEW CLAIMS EMERGE DURING CRITICAL SENATE BATTLE The ad’s post on X was widely mocked by Democrats and Republicans and has been viewed over 2 million times. "Maine is the oldest median age electorate in the nation," Democratic strategist Steve Schale posted on X. "I know I’m not a DC strategist but I really, really don’t get it." "Troy Jackson needs to win but videos like this are unhelpful and cringey," liberal influencer Harry Sisson posted on X. "Please change it up! No boba tea!" "The same people that ran Mallory McMorrow's campaign into the ground are telling you to do this goofy s---," left-wing podcaster Kyle Kulinski posted on X. "Just get out there and tell the truth and speak from the heart for economic justice and against war and stop with all this bulls---. C'mon man. You're smarter than this." DEM SENATE NOMINEE BREAKS SILENCE AFTER SUSAN COLLINS' OFFICE WAS VANDALIZED WITH VULGAR MESSAGE "It's a little bit funny to be desperately trying to position as working class masculine male and have gen-z women run your socials like they would run their own personals," Republican communicator Matt Whitlock posted on X. "... ," National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) Southern regional press secretary Reilly Richardson posted on X. " Weird," GOP communicator Steve Guest posted on X. "Looks like the first time that Troy Jackson has ever had boba." "Boba tea! Just like regular people! " journalist Chris Cillizza posted on X. "Want to remind you that Democrats were openly proud of how masculine their Maine campaign was going to be and then they ran this ad," former Trump campaign communications director Tim Murtaugh posted on X. Fox News Digital reached out to Jackson's campaign for comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A recent poll indicates Collins is ahead of her Democratic challenger in a crucial Senate showdown in blue-leaning Maine that could determine the balance of power in the U.S. Senate. Collins, who is running for a sixth six-year term in the Senate, stands at 49% support among likely voters, with former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee, at 46%, with 5% undecided in the New York Times/Siena poll. Collins' three-point edge is within the survey's margin of error. The survey, which was conducted Sept. 15–22, is one of the first to indicate Collins ahead of Jackson since he replaced former Senate nominee Graham Platner in late July. Platner, a combat veteran and oyster farmer, won the June Democratic Senate primary in a landslide. But a month later he dropped out following an explosive report containing an allegation of rape from a woman he previously dated. Platner denied the report but stepped aside. Collins slightly trailed Platner in most polling at the time he ended his campaign. Jackson, who campaigned alongside Platner earlier this year as he unsuccessfully ran for governor, won a special nominating convention to fill the party's vacant Senate nomination. The poll release came as Collins pushed back against a report by ProPublica that the FBI sought to launch a pay-to-play investigation examining Collins and others. The investigation was later dropped and no one working for Collins was charged. Collins ripped the report as "offensive" and a "partisan hit job" orchestrated by Democrats. Jackson took to social media to claim that "Susan Collins is blatantly corrupt." Collins' advantage over Jackson in the new survey comes even as 55% of those questioned said they prefer Democrats to control the Senate next year, with 43% saying they'd like the GOP to retain the majority. Fox News Digital's Paul Steinhauser contributed to this report.

articles.title: LEE CARTER: Trump can still get attention, can he distract voters from their bills?
articles.summary: Trump's approval on inflation sits at just 24% as polls show 62% of voters call grocery prices a major problem ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
articles.body: President Donald Trump has never suffered from an attention deficit. Ours, maybe. His, never. For more than a decade, Trump has demonstrated an almost supernatural ability to decide what America will talk about. A nickname. A Truth Social post. A feud. A rally. A tariff. A threat. A late-night broadside against somebody who had the gall to criticize him. TO WIN IN NOVEMBER, REPUBLICANS NEED TO TAKE A PAGE FROM OBAMA’S PLAYBOOK Trump throws the ball and Washington and the media chase it. But something interesting is happening as we head toward the midterms. REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY. The country may be getting tired of chasing. The latest Fox News poll contains a number that should be flashing in giant red letters inside the White House: Asked, without being given a list, to name the most important issue facing the country, 34% of registered voters said the cost of living. Another 14% said the economy and jobs. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: WHAT’S IN AN ECONOMY? Nothing else came close. Immigration was at 8%. The war with Iran, 4%. AI and data centers, despite consuming approximately 94% of the oxygen in corporate America, registered at 1%. Voters are not being subtle. IT’S NOT THE ECONOMY, STUPID. AMERICANS VOTE BASED ON THEIR PERSONAL ECONOMY They are saying: It's the prices. Stupid. And yet much of the political conversation seems to be happening somewhere else. REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE Trump is battling the media. He is talking about his predecessor. He is dealing with Iran, China, immigration and AI. Some of those issues are enormously consequential. Presidents do not get to spend their days staring at the price of eggs. But voters don't experience the presidency as a policy seminar. RECORD GAS PRICES SQUEEZE AMERICANS AS SUMMER TRAVEL SEASON ENDS, MIDTERMS LOOM AND IRAN WAR WAGES ON They experience it at the grocery store. The latest Fox News poll contains a number that should be flashing in giant red letters inside the White House: Asked, without being given a list, to name the most important issue facing the country, 34% of registered voters said the cost of living. Another 14% said the economy and jobs. At the gas pump. THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE When the utility bill arrives. When they look at what it costs to buy a house, see a doctor or fill their grocery cart. BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT And on those questions, the Fox numbers are difficult for the administration. Sixty-two percent say grocery prices are a major problem. Sixty-one percent say the same about gas prices. Fifty-four percent say it about housing. Fifty-two percent about health care. And 63% say the Trump administration has made the economy worse. The administration can point to its own economic strength data. Employment has remained resilient, and the stock market has performed strongly. Fox's own analysis recently noted job growth and unemployment of 4.1%. But this is where presidents (and politicians writ large) discover one of the more irritating rules of politics: You don't get to tell voters how they feel about the economy. They tell you. That was true for President Joe Biden. It is true for Donald Trump. Biden spent much of his presidency pointing to macroeconomic statistics that were considerably healthier than the public mood. Inflation was coming down. Jobs were being created. The economy had avoided the recession many economists predicted. And voters kept saying some version of: That's lovely. Do you know how much a dozen eggs cost? Trump understood that disconnect better than almost anyone. He turned economic frustration into political fuel. Now he owns the podium. Which means he also owns the problem. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found only 17% of U.S. adults approved of Trump's handling of the cost of living. His overall approval was 32% in that survey. Fox, polling registered voters with a different methodology, put his overall approval at 39% and his approval on inflation at 24%. Different polls, different populations, same warning light: affordability is a major vulnerability for the administration. Presidents do not get to spend their days staring at the price of eggs. But voters don't experience the presidency as a policy seminar. They experience it at the grocery store. This is where Trump's greatest communications strength can become a weakness. He understands attention better than perhaps any political figure of the modern era. He knows how to interrupt. He knows how to provoke. He knows how to make himself the main character. But attention and persuasion are not the same thing. Attention is getting everyone to look at you. Persuasion is getting them to look at the problem differently. And right now, voters appear to have a problem they don't particularly want changed. They want it solved. There is another revealing number buried in the Fox poll. Democrats currently hold a 15-point advantage over Republicans when voters are asked which party they trust more on inflation. But the same poll offers an important qualification: voters who trust Democrats on inflation are slightly more likely to say it is because Republicans have failed than because they believe Democratic policies will lower prices. That isn't exactly a love letter to either party. It's an eviction notice to whoever voters think isn't listening. And that's why the midterm communications challenge may be simpler than Washington is making it. Trump doesn't need another subject. He has one. Affordability. Every other argument can run through it. China? What does competing with China mean for American jobs and prices? AI? What does it mean for my paycheck and electric bill? Iran? What does a prolonged conflict mean for gasoline and the cost of moving goods around the country? Taxes and tariffs? What will I pay? The communications opportunity isn't necessarily to talk less about the world. It's to translate the world into the lives people are actually living. Trump's political genius has always been his instinct for finding the thing people are feeling before the political establishment figures out how to talk about it. In 2016, that was disruption. Trump understood that disconnect better than almost anyone. He turned economic frustration into political fuel. Now he owns the podium. Which means he also owns the problem. In 2024, it was frustration with prices, immigration and the direction of the country. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION In 2026, voters are once again telling Washington exactly what's bothering them. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The question is whether Washington is listening. Trump can still make America look. The harder task now is convincing Americans that he's looking at what they're looking at. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM LEE CARTER

articles.title: Trump to begin sending $500 ACA refund checks to 1 million Americans
articles.summary: Nearly 1 million Americans will begin receiving $500 Obamacare refund checks on Sept. 30, along with letters signed by President Donald Trump.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump is set on Sept. 30 to start sending $500 checks to nearly 1 million Americans his administration says were overcharged through the Affordable Care Act's federal exchange for buying health insurance.

Treasury Department checks, along with letters signed by Trump notifying recipients, will begin going out to more than 950,000 Americans across 30 states, according to an administration official.

"For years, the Biden administration overcharged you to fund the operation of HealthCare.gov," Trump says in the letter, which was viewed by USA TODAY. "That money belongs to hard-working Americans, not the Government, and now I'm returning it to you!"

Donald Trump's second term: Actions, travels of the 47th president

President Donald Trump is pictured at his Trump International Golf Club on the final day's play at the Amgen Irish Open on Sept.13, 2026 in Doonbeg, Ireland. U.S. President Donald Trump is making a two-day visit to Ireland this weekend. Today his trip focuses on attending the Amgen Irish Open golf tournament, which is being hosted at his Doonbeg golf resort.

Trump announced the $500 Obamacare refund checks on Sept. 10 in a video posted by the White House that coincided with the Republican midterm convention in Dallas. The money is separate from a controversial $5,000 dividend Trump has vowed to distribute to all Americans if Republicans retain control of Congress after the November midterm election.

The White House has said the Biden administration collected user fees from health insurance companies that consumers paid for in the form of higher premiums ‒ and that the premiums exceeded what was needed to run the exchange. The Trump administration has accused the Biden administration of sitting on the surplus of money.

The checks, issued five weeks before the November midterm election, come as Americans' anxieties over high costs and affordability pose major political liabilities for Trump Republicans as they look to hold on to power in Congress.

"You have paid into this flawed System, and now you are finally getting something back," Trump says in the letter.

The expiration of the enhanced ACA subsidies at the end of 2025, which Trump and Republicans in Congress refused to extend, made insurance more expensive for millions of consumers.

Trump headlines first-of-its-kind GOP election convention in Dallas

The interior of the American Airlines Center is seen on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention on Sept. 9, 2026 in Dallas, Texas. Republicans are kicking off two days of political pageantry aimed at blunting Democrats' momentum in the battle for control of Congress, holding their first-ever midterm election convention ‒ headlined tonight by President Donald Trump ‒ in a bid to boost GOP enthusiasm amid warning signs for the party. Trump is rallying Republicans for the final push toward the Nov. 3 election with a big show in the Lone Star State featuring a long list of party leaders and candidates in swing districts.

The president's approval rating has sagged as the Iran war drags on and cost-of-living concerns remain top of mind for many voters, threatening to weigh down GOP candidates. Trump has turned to the mini-convention to provide a boost as the party struggles to sell his second-term agenda.

The 30 states where some Americans will receive refund checks are states that do not operate their own ACA insurance plan exchanges and rely on federal exchanges administered by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, according to the White House.

The 30 states are Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Hawaii, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming.

Americans in the other 20 states won't receive checks because their states run their exchanges and the federal government did not collect user fees.

Most recipients are people who earn about 400% of the federal poverty line ‒ $64,000 for a single person or $132,000 for a family of four ‒ but it includes some people between 100-400% of the federal poverty line, the White House said.

"I am proud to return your money to you, and I will never stop fighting to put the American People FIRST, restore Affordability, protect your hard-earned money, and lower the Cost of Healthcare," Trump says in the letter. "May God bless you, and may He continue to bless the United States of America."

Contributing: Bart Jansen and Ken Alltucker , USA TODAY

articles.title: California poll: Voters back a billionaire tax, but the proposal falls short of majority support
articles.summary: A new NBCUniversal Local/Telemundo Station Group shows “yes” supporters leading 48% to 38% on the California ballot measure.
articles.body: A plurality of likely California voters support a proposal on the state’s November ballot that would impose a one-time wealth tax on the richest Californians, but the measure is still short of majority support, according to a new NBCUniversal Local/Telemundo Station Group poll released Wednesday. In the poll, 48% said they would vote “yes” on the proposal, while 38% said they would vote “no.” Another 14% said they were undecided. The 10-point lead for “yes” is outside the poll’s margin of error, which is plus or minus 4 percentage points for each side’s support level. The spread was almost identical among Hispanic likely voters, according to a companion survey of California: 50% said they’d vote “yes,” 40% said they’d vote “no,” and 10% said they were undecided. Both surveys were conducted Sept. 21-24. The so-called billionaire tax — which will appear on the November ballot as “Proposition 40” — would implement a one-time 5% tax on the assets of Californians with net worths exceeding $1.1 billion, and it would require the state to spend 90% of the new revenue on healthcare. The remaining 10% would be split between education and food assistance programs. In addition to the one-time tax on those worth more than $1.1 billion, the measure, if it is passed, would implement a smaller tax on individuals worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion. The taxes would apply retroactively to anyone living in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026. The proposal has divided Democratic leaders in California. Prominent proponents — including Rep. Ro Khanna, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, and Tom Steyer, a billionaire activist who unsuccessfully ran for governor — argue it would help close income inequality gaps and help make up for state budget shortfalls as a result of Medicaid cuts in President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill.” Opponents of the ballot measure, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and the Democratic candidate to succeed him this year, Xavier Becerra, have argued the initiative would drive wealthy investors and tech leaders from the state. The details of the proposal, which has been led by Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, a large California healthcare workers union, have also sparked opposition from many other unions and Democratic groups. Those groups have taken issue with the fact that other progressive policy priorities, like public education and food assistance, would benefit far less than healthcare from the new revenue. Many Democratic critics have also joined forces with some Republicans, many of whom have long argued that a wealth tax could destabilize California’s revenue streams by causing the ultrarich to flee the state. But the new poll showed California voters were largely not worried about the prospect of wealthy California residents’ leaving. A total of 59% of respondents said they were either “not” or “not too” concerned about that potential outcome, while a total of 41% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned about rich people’s leaving the state because of the ballot measure. Among Hispanic voters, 62% said they were either “not” or “not too” concerned, while 38% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned. Notably, the poll also found California voters almost evenly split over whether they approve or disapprove of the job performance of Newsom, widely seen as a 2028 presidential hopeful. Forty-five percent of respondents said they approved of his job performance, while 46% said they disapproved. Another 9% said they weren’t sure. Hispanic voters were more positive about Newsom, with 54% approving and 38% disapproving of his performance as governor. But when it came to how Democrats felt about a possible Newsom 2028 bid, they overwhelmingly said they’d get behind him. Asked whether they’d be inclined to vote for him if he ran to become the Democratic Party’s presidential nominee in 2028, 66% of Democratic respondents said yes, 15% said no, and 19% said they weren’t sure. Another November ballot measure, Proposition 39, would, if it is passed, require voters to show a government-issued ID when they cast ballots in person, while mail-in voters would have to provide the last four digits of a designated ID used during registration. Among likely voters, 49% said they would support the measure, while 42% said they would vote against it, and 9% said they were undecided. Asked about Proposition 39, 55% of Hispanic voters said they would vote “yes” in support of it, while 38% said they would vote “no,” and 7% said they were undecided. California voters strongly said cost of living and the economy were among the most important issues when they were deciding to vote, with 25% saying “cost of living/inflation” was the most important and 23% saying “economy/jobs.” Another 15% said “immigration and enforcement” was the most important, while 11% said healthcare, and 10% said “foreign policy and the Iran War.” No other issue registered at more than 5%. Amid the focus on economic issues, a plurality of respondents — 42% — said their “personal financial situation” was “the same” as four years earlier. Thirty-six percent said it was “worse” compared with four years earlier, while 22% said it was “better.” Meanwhile, most respondents (64%) in reliably blue California overwhelmingly said they disapproved of the job President Donald Trump was doing. Another 31% said they approved, and 5% said they weren’t sure. Asked how much impact they felt the conflict with Iran was having on the U.S. economy, more than two-thirds (67%) of respondents said it was having a “great” deal of impact. Another 16% said it was having “some” impact, while 7% said “not much,” and 8% said “none.”

articles.title: Inside the neighborhood living on the edge of America’s tech frontier
articles.summary: Loudoun County homeowners on Statesboro Place describe constant noise from Amazon Web Services and Microsoft data centers just 150 feet from backyards.
articles.body: ASHBURN, Va. — First came the explosions, the heavy machinery and the red dust that coated the neighborhood. Soon after, towering, windowless buildings emerged just beyond a thin row of trees. Months after the construction noise faded, the silence gave way to a steady mechanical hum. For homeowners on the tucked-away cul-de-sac of Statesboro Place in Loudoun County, Virginia, suburban life now shares a fence line with the infrastructure powering America's artificial intelligence (AI) boom. The facilities behind the neighborhood are operated by Amazon Web Services and Microsoft, two of the world's largest cloud computing companies. "It's like 150 feet away and just constant noise," one resident told Fox News Digital while looking out over the backyard on a rainy September afternoon. "So far, they've planted some trees, thinking that would solve the issue." A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD’S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES A Microsoft spokesperson told Fox News Digital the company is "actively meeting with nearby HOAs to address community priorities, including landscaping, lighting and noise, working to ensure that our development lives up to residents' expectations." An Amazon spokesperson said the company has "been part of Loudoun for 20 years" and that its local team has been working directly with residents and the HOA to address concerns. "We’re committed to building responsibly and being good neighbors," the spokesperson said. The residents interviewed for this story requested anonymity as they are engaged in ongoing discussions with the HOA and county officials. One resident, who bought the home nearly a decade ago, said the hum extends beyond the backyards and can be heard along the community's walking trails. "Only two data centers are active right now and two additional ones are planned to be active next spring," the resident said, adding that neighbors fear the noise will only grow louder. The neighborhood sits in Loudoun County, home to the world's largest concentration of data centers and one of the epicenters of the nation's AI infrastructure buildout. Residents say they were drawn to the spacious lots, unobstructed views and quiet streets, all of which are now overshadowed by featureless buildings. THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS As of March 2026, more than 230 data centers had been built or were under construction across the Virginia county, with another 116 projects in the pipeline. "When I moved in, it was an open field. I had a nice backyard and there was not an ugly building to look at," another resident told Fox News Digital. The resident says the question isn't whether data centers should exist, but whether they belong so close to neighborhoods without a better understanding of how they affect the people living beside them. "Are we the guinea pigs? It feels that way." The data centers that transformed the landscape have also reshaped Loudoun County's finances. County officials say data centers generated $1.2 billion in tax revenue in fiscal year 2026 — 39% of the county budget — and project that figure will rise to $1.3 billion in fiscal year 2027. The revenue helps fund county services and keep tax rates lower, but residents say their individual bills have continued to rise. One Loudoun County homeowner shared six years of property tax records with Fox News Digital showing the annual real estate tax bill rose from $17,391 in 2021 to about $22,250 in 2026, an increase of nearly $5,000. "In our experience, our taxes have not gone down. We also own multiple properties and vehicles in Loudoun County, and we have not experienced a reduction in our real estate or personal property tax burden," the homeowner said. The bill can rise even when tax rates fall if the assessed value increases. ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM That disconnect has raised questions about whether the industry’s financial benefits outweigh its impact on nearby communities. Little River District Supervisor Laura TeKrony said Loudoun County should limit data center development to industrial areas. "I have not voted for one data center application since my term started in 2024," TeKrony told Fox News Digital. "There are some things that matter more than additional tax revenue: our land, our water, our quality of life and our community character." AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY Residents told Fox News Digital they recognize the data centers are unlikely to go away. articles.title: Senate hopeful's 'treading water' narrative crumbles under $500K campaign payouts to family
articles.summary: Dan Osborn's campaign has paid over $500,000 to family members even as the Nebraska Senate candidate claims his family is "treading water."
articles.body: Independent Senate candidate Dan Osborn repeatedly said his family is "treading water" financially because of rising grocery and gas prices last week, but federal campaign finance records show his campaign has paid more than $500,000 to members of his family since launching his Senate bid. Speaking at a Capitol Hill press conference on Sept. 24, Osborn said, "My family, we're treading water here, and it feels like every day it's hard to keep your head above water" because of the economy and rising grocery and gas prices. Later that day, during an NBC News interview, he made nearly identical remarks, again describing his family as "treading water." Americans for Public Trust, a government ethics watchdog that has previously scrutinized Osborn's campaign spending, estimates Osborn and members of his family received nearly $480,000 from his campaign and affiliated PACs through the first quarter of 2026. The organization told Fox News Digital that figure does not include additional campaign spending disclosed in Osborn's second-quarter filing, which was filed in July. Fox News Digital's review of that filing found additional payments to family members that pushed the total above $500,000. NEBRASKA SENATE CANDIDATE SEEMS TO CONFIRM AUDIO CLAIMING TRUMP SUPPORTERS' LIVES 'SUCK SO F---ING BAD' The largest share of those payments went to Osborn's wife, Megan Osborn, who has worked for the campaign since its launch. Campaign finance records also show payments to the candidate's daughter, Georgia, who Osborn has described publicly as a part-time dancer who still needs help paying her bills. His daughter has been paid by the campaign for work including event staffing and campaign activities, alongside other relatives and entities tied to his family. Amid the scrutiny, Osborn's wife stepped away from consulting firms she had a stake in, which were receiving thousands of dollars from Osborn's campaign coffers, including from his 2024 war chest, even though that campaign was defunct. "It’s rich for Osborn to be co-opting the real financial pain of Nebraskans when he and his family have been profiting from his campaign since it launched," Americans for Public Trust Executive Director Caitlin Sutherland told Fox News Digital. "He was all too comfortable using his campaign to enrich his immediate and extended family and only hastily restructured when he was caught. Nebraskans know better than to fall for this type of self-serving behavior." DEM SENATOR FACES DOJ PROBE AFTER ALLEGATIONS OF SPENDING CAMPAIGN FUNDS ON LUXURY LIFESTYLE Earlier this year, Osborn and his wife announced they were restructuring how she was compensated by the campaign after Americans for Public Trust filed a complaint with the Federal Election Commission alleging Osborn had steered campaign funds to relatives through a network of consulting firms and affiliated political action committees. The complaint alleged the payments violated federal campaign finance law, while the Osborn campaign rejected the allegations and argued the payments were for legitimate campaign work. While paying family members is not illegal, it must be for bona-fide campaign services. Critics have challenged the political expertise and background of Osborn's wife and other family members. As part of the restructuring, Osborn's wife stepped away from two consulting firms that were receiving campaign payments — including Independent Campaigns LLC, in which she held a one-third ownership stake — and instead became the campaign's full-time operations manager with a monthly salary. Osborn told the Omaha World-Herald at the time that his wife had been "instrumental" to the campaign and said he would not let political opponents dictate who ran it. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But Sutherland argued the restructuring did not resolve the broader questions raised in the complaint. "Dan Osborn only restructured how he pays his wife after we filed a complaint with the FEC that he was running afoul of campaign finance laws," Sutherland told Fox News Digital at the time. "However, questions still remain regarding his payments to his daughter, his brother-in-law, and two sisters-in-law, and his control over two federal PACs. Rest assured, Osborn may have changed tactics, but he isn't off the hook in his attempt to funnel campaign cash to his entire family."

articles.title: A blue wave is rising, but after November, it’s sink or swim for Democratic insurgents
articles.summary: Calling for change is one thing — actually delivering on it is another beast altogether.
articles.body:
There’s just over a month left in a midterm campaign season that feels like it has dragged on forever, and as Politico’s Jonathan Martin opined last week , the polling cliff facing Republicans has grown so dire that “the only uncertainty remaining ahead of the midterms is the depth of the party’s losses.” That’s hardly the message President Trump and his MAGA minions hoped to end with when they weighed a defensible red electoral map late last year.

Washington’s Democratic leaders are also facing their own moment of reckoning. More incumbent Democrats have lost their primaries than at any time since 1992, and the candidates who have replaced them are promising a sweeping policy agenda coupled with a pledge to shake up the party’s House and Senate leadership.

But calling for change is one thing — actually delivering on it is another beast altogether.

After years of missed opportunities to claim real gains under Presidents Obama and Biden, voters are sick of waiting. Democratic outsiders, like Texas’s James Talarico, Maine’s Troy Jackson, Michigan’s Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan and a host of other rising stars, are channeling voters’ frustration by acknowledging that change under Democrats has often come so slowly that it often feels like nothing is moving at all.

Their plan even looks beyond 2026 to the pivotal presidential contest in 2028, when insurgent Democrats may have a golden opportunity to elevate one of their own to the White House. That’s partly because even the most ambitious reformer doesn’t expect much progress from a Democratic Congress hobbled at every turn by a recalcitrant White House. If Republicans go down in flames in November, as polls increasingly suggest they will , Trump will be in no mood to work with the Democrats who battered his MAGA coalition. El-Sayed and company could succeed in electing an outsider to replace Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer only to find their next two years jammed with shutdown standoffs and budgetary gridlock.

Democrats may find narrow areas of policy overlap with Trump, like their shared desire to claim a populist victory by banning Wall Street firms from buying up residential homes or barring lawmakers from trading stock (despite Trump being perhaps the most prolific stock trader in the presidency’s history). But those compromises won’t come cheap, and any cooperation with the White House will likely come with a healthy dose of scorn from a Democratic base that views any collaboration with Trump as a betrayal of the highest order.

Would Talarico or Jackson have the grit to accept a ban on politicians trading stock and an end to Wall Street homebuying in exchange for a big boost to ICE funding? It’s unclear, but seems highly unlikely given the campaigns they are currently running and the longer-term goals they desire from a Democratic administration beyond 2029.

Insurgent Democrats may find an unlikely ally in Schumer.

It’s widely expected that the long-serving New Yorker will not seek another six-year term, but the Old Man of the Senate is still acutely sensitive to his legacy. Schumer has clearly learned a lesson from his bitter and unsuccessful proxy battle to defeat El-Sayed in the Michigan primary, and recently tried to mend fences by dispatching $10 million in superPAC money to bolster El-Sayed’s general election chances. With most of the Democratic base now rallying behind the very outsiders he failed to beat, Schumer may find it more advantageous to embrace the kind of “ big-tent populism ” that defines political legacies instead of trying to force his own way forward.

If Democrats’ contingent of Senate outsiders can convince the party’s rattled establishment leaders to grant them political cover as they develop their signature proposals into actual policies, they may find the breathing room necessary to be effective lawmakers. Without that buy-in, though, Democrats will once again find themselves holding power and yet fighting among themselves for the microphone.

Keeping the temperamental Democratic base from losing faith will be a key test of the new lawmakers’ skills. Voters love Talarico’s proposed “ New American Dream” program, a huge bundle of anticorruption and quality of life bills that would reshape federal ethics laws and address the mounting affordability crisis. But are they willing to wait until 2029 at the earliest for Talarico’s biggest priorities to get a real hearing under a possible Democratic president?

Democratic voters are upset, frustrated, anxious and angry about the slow pace of change in their party. Their most effective politicians have harnessed those emotions to generate a record amount of voter enthusiasm ahead of one of the most consequential elections of our lifetime. Winning will be the first step, but developing a real plan for using their power will be Priority No.1 once the polls close on Election Day.

Max Burns is a veteran Democratic strategist and founder of Third Degree Strategies.

articles.title: Paxton: Trump GOP midterm convention ‘dropped our numbers’
articles.summary: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate in the Lone Star State, said that the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas hurt him politically. “So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good,” Paxton said…
articles.body:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate in the Lone Star State, said that the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas hurt him politically.

“So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good,” Paxton said in an audio clip shared by The New York Times. He’d been asked whether he felt that “he’s a little bit of a drag,” though whom the questioner was referring to was unclear in the recording.

Paxton made the remark at a private fundraiser in Washington, D.C., attended by conservative donors and lobbyists, according to the Times.

Nick Maddux, a senior Paxton adviser, told The Hill that “this is more manipulated nonsense from The New York Times to create a story that doesn’t exist.”

Maddux pointed to polling that’s shown Paxton ahead, arguing that “every serious pollster will tell you that our numbers have improved since early September” and that Paxton “is going to win this race.”

Paxton is also expected to attend Trump’s Thursday trip to Denton, Texas.

The Trump-backed Republican was a major focus of the Republican National Committee’s first-ever midterm convention in Dallas earlier this month, a two-day bash aimed at reinvigorating the base.

The president sought to elevate Paxton, who defeated incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a bitter primary runoff and is now trailing Democrat James Talarico by 2 percentage points ahead of the general election, according to Decision Desk HQ’s latest polling averages, though it remains unclear at this point whether the convention directly impacted Paxton’s polling outlook.

In a closing-night convention speech, Trump gave a double-edged pitch for Paxton, saying he doesn’t “like the way Ken dresses,” “talks” or “looks,” but that the Senate hopeful is “the greatest” attorney general in the country.

“I don’t know if he’s going to ever speak to me again, but you know, I don’t care as long as he wins,” Trump told the Dallas crowd. “I don’t have to speak to him. He’s going to vote the way we would vote. … You got to vote for him.”

Paxton, whose scandal-plagued tenure as the top Texas prosecutor made him a controversial Senate pick, also addressed the convention, asking the audience for “your prayers” and “your votes.”

Though Democrats have struggled for decades to win statewide in red Texas, Paxton’s race against Talarico is now considered a toss-up.

“This is embarrassing for the President. Texans know that Paxton is a cheater, who only serves his own corrupt self interests, and now Trump gets to experience it firsthand,” Texas Democratic Party spokesperson Ryan Martin said in a statement.

articles.title: We lose an hour of daylight (or more) in October: How short your days will get
articles.summary: Darker days are ahead as winter inches every closer. But just how short are days about to feel?
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Fall is officially here, with winter just on the horizon. Regardless of the weather near you , you may have already noticed one of the trademarks of fall: the days are getting shorter .

It’s a trend that has been ongoing since summer, but it becomes arguably more noticeable in fall. Many regions have already experienced their last sunset after 7 p.m. until spring , with more to follow soon.

Through October, many of us will lose at least an hour of daylight in our days.

As we progress through winter, Earth’s tilt and orbit mean the sun hits the northern hemisphere more indirectly, cutting back the daylight we get.

Those living in the northern portion of the U.S. stand to lose the most daylight through October. In Bismarck, North Dakota, and Portland, Oregon, for example, there is more than a 90-minute difference between how long Oct. 1 and Oct. 31 are (in terms of daylight), as you can see in the table below.

Meanwhile, Honolulu will lose only about 34 minutes of daylight by the time Halloween hits.

At present, Honolulu gets almost 12 hours of daylight, with the sun rising around 6:23 a.m. and setting just before 6:20 p.m. By the end of October, those times will shift to 6:34 a.m. and 5:56 p.m., respectively.

The end of October will also bring another upending change: the end of daylight saving time. We, in a way, get an extra hour on Nov. 1 when the clocks “fall back” an hour . We’ll also see the sun rise and set an hour earlier than it does on Halloween.

That may be moot, though, should the Senate pass the Sunshine Protection Act. The bill, which has received President Trump’s support since passing through the House, would make daylight saving time permanent . While you would notice an impact during winter, the move would not add to the amount of daylight hours we experience.

Unless the Senate takes up and passes the Sunshine Protection Act soon, you can expect your clocks to fall back an hour on Nov. 1.

articles.title: No, claims against Judge Altman never needed a special committee
articles.summary: It is hardly fair to blame a judge for following the rules.
articles.body:
Steven Lubet recently argued it was a mistake for the chief judge of the U.S. 11th Circuit Court of Appeals to dismiss a complaint against Judge Roy Altman. But he got the whole thing very wrong.

Lubet argued that whether Altman’s media interviews were a “substantial” use of government resources may be “reasonably disputed.” Therefore, he reasoned, the matter have gone to a special committee under the Rules for Judicial-Conduct and Judicial-Disability Proceedings . For this, he relies on the commentary appended to those rules.

But the commentary is quite clear that the purpose of a special committee is to resolve disputed questions of fact. “If it is clear that the conduct or disability alleged, even if true, is not cognizable under these rules, the complaint should be dismissed,” it reads.

The commentary also notes that its standards are “used to decide motions for summary judgment,” and “genuine issues of material fact are not resolved at the summary judgment stage.”

The facts of this case are not in dispute. Altman acknowledges that he gave “podcast or TV interviews in [his] judicial chambers on thirteen separate days over several months.” Lubet does not identify any fact about these interviews that is contested. Instead, he asks whether “the question of substantiality” is “relative or absolute,” and says “an investigating committee might well conclude that the broadcasts were sufficiently regular and repeated to be objectively substantial in and of themselves. Or they might ask whether a judge should be making even one sales pitch from chambers.”

But none of that is a factual dispute that would defeat a summary judgment motion. Therefore, a special committee is not required. Whether “substantiality” is relative or absolute is an interpretive question of law, as opposed to a question of fact — for example, how much time Altman spent on judicial work in his chambers.

Whether broadcasts that are “sufficiently regular and repeated” count as “substantial” under the rules is likewise a legal question, not a factual one. And whether “a judge should be making even one sales pitch from chambers” is an argument about what the rules ought to say, not a dispute about what actually happened.

Altman’s statements about keffiyehs are not factually disputed, either. They are thus equally unsuited for a special committee.

The commentary provides that “dismissal following a limited inquiry may occur when a complaint refers to transcripts or to witnesses and the chief judge determines that the transcripts and witnesses all support the subject judge.”

Thus, it is misleading to claim that “a special committee … could have reviewed Altman’s Middle East Forum interview.” The chief judge reviewing a “transcript” of a media interview is the very example given by the commentary of what can be resolved without a special committee.

The assertion that that a judge should not be making “even one sales pitch from chambers” is not the law, either. Committee on Codes of Conduct Advisory Opinion No. 79 is directly on point: “A judge may use judicial resources such as the library, chambers, and computers for compensated activity so long as this use is within reasonable limits and the government incurs no incremental cost.”

Lubet does not even acknowledge this advisory opinion, much less attempt to rebut it. Altman was entitled not only to make a “sales pitch” from chambers, but even to charge for each interview.

Nothing in the public record indicates that Altman used judicial personnel to support his compensated activity, that the activity exceeded reasonable limits or that it interfered with his official duties. And the use of the court’s always-available internet connection imposes no incremental cost on the government.

One can fairly question whether Lubet is not applying a double standard, since Altman is hardly the first judge to write a book. In 2024 alone, Supreme Court justices banked over $10 million in book sales , with Justice Sonia Sotomayor bringing in nearly $4 million and Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson collecting a $3 million advance for her memoir. Shortly after that memoir was published, USA Today released an interview with Justice Jackson in her chambers, which repeatedly mentioned her book.

Lubet makes much of Altman’s self-identification as a judge in media interviews, but it says nothing about Judge Richard Posner, who authored over 30 books and repeatedly gave television interviews about those books as “Judge Richard Posner.”

To be clear, I am one of many who enjoy reading (and purchasing) books written by judges. But if one’s goal is to rid the judiciary of book-sale income, one might start with the Supreme Court rather than a district judge in Florida.

Anyone is entitled to believe that judges must write books for free. But Lubet should have at least acknowledged that the law is on Altman’s side. It is hardly fair to blame a judge for following the rules.

Joshua Mitts is the David J. Greenwald Professor of Law at Columbia University.

articles.title: Senate Democrats rip DHS over diverted funding for campaign-style Trump ads
articles.summary: Two Democratic senators are demanding answers following reports that Department of Homeland Security (DHS) funds were used to run TV advertisements promoting President Trump. In a Tuesday letter addressed to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Sens. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) and Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) asked him to address several questions regarding the use of the funds within…
articles.body:
Two Democratic senators are demanding answers following reports that Department of Homeland Security (DHS) funds were used to run TV advertisements promoting President Trump.

In a Tuesday letter addressed to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Sens. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) and Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) asked him to address several questions regarding the use of the funds within 48 hours.

“The American people deserve answers about how this president is literally stealing their tax dollars to air campaign ads celebrating himself — while doing nothing to help them afford health care or housing,” the Democrats wrote.

“These ads need to immediately come off the air, taxpayers need to be paid back for this theft, and everyone responsible needs to be held accountable for this corrupt and illegal propaganda,” they continued.

The 30-second ad features Trump saying, “Together, we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America” while the song “Love Me” by JMSN plays in the background.

The commercial has drawn criticism from both Democratic and Republican lawmakers, with Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) saying the ad violated the Hatch Act.

In the letter, Murray and Murphy asked the DHS secretary to provide a breakdown of how department funds were used in the production of the TV spots and for more information about who directed the fund transfer.

The lawmakers cited an estimate from AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm, that the administration has spent more than $1.7 million to run the ads on national TV networks.

When reached for comment, DHS referred The Hill to a White House statement defending the commercials as “public service announcements” and slamming criticism of the ads as “highly dishonest.”

“The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action,” the statement reads. “Instead, the announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending — at home, at the border and abroad.”

The president has repeatedly called on voters to “pretend” that he is “on the ballot” this November when voting in the midterm elections. Trump also promised to pay out $5,000 to every American adult if the GOP maintains its control of both chambers of Congress this fall.

The Democrats said the Trump administration’s defense of the new ads is “as absurd as it is offensive” and cited recent opposition from a GOP lawmaker in their letter.

“The White House has failed to answer our most basic questions about where these funds are coming from and who is responsible, but the principle here is very straightforward: as one Republican senator put it: ‘you can’t spend public money to promote yourself,’” they wrote.

On Sunday, Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told CBS News’s “Face the Nation” host Margaret Brennan that Trump and other public officials should not “spend public money on private ads for themselves.”

“The White House sees it differently, but … you can’t spend public money to promote yourself,” the Louisiana Republican said.
