articles.title: Federal appeals court stays Christa Pike execution with hours to spare
articles.summary: A federal appeals court on Wednesday halted the execution of Christa Pike around an hour before it was scheduled to occur. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit issued a short stay of execution order to permit time “to properly analyze the parties’ fully briefed arguments and resolve the issues on the merits.”…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court on Wednesday halted the execution of Christa Pike around an hour before it was scheduled to occur.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit issued a short stay of execution order to permit time “to properly analyze the parties’ fully briefed arguments and resolve the issues on the merits.”

Pike was set to be executed by lethal injection at 10 a.m. local time Wednesday at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. She would have been the first woman executed in the state of Tennessee in 200 years.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court denied a request to stop Pike’s execution without explanation. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) also said earlier this week he would not grant clemency in the case.

Pike was convicted of first-degree murder in 1996 for the killing of her 19-year-old classmate, Colleen Slemmer. Prosecutors said that Pike and her boyfriend at the time lured Slemmer to an abandoned steam plant near the University of Tennessee agricultural campus and then beat, tortured and killed her.

Pike confessed to the murder and admitted that she had slashed Slemmer’s throat several times, threw asphalt at her head and kept a piece of her skull as a souvenir, according to court documents.

Her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, received a lifetime prison sentence and was not eligible for the death penalty since he was 17 years old at the time of the murder. His parole was denied last year.

Federal public defenders for Pike argued that she was subjected to “extreme sexual abuse” throughout her childhood and that this history was not fully presented to the jury during her sentencing.

Pike has since been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder and bipolar disorder, and she described herself as a “mentally ill 18-year-old kid” in her state clemency petition.

She was also convicted on another count of attempted first-degree murder in the 2001 assault of fellow inmate Patricia Jones, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction.

Tennessee has appealed the appeals court’s stay order to the Supreme Court.

The Hill’s Sophie Brams contributed reporting.

articles.title: Bessent is wrong: China armed Iran’s nuclear weapons ambitions
articles.summary: Secretary Bessent, it is China that has made Iran dangerous.
articles.body:
“In terms of China, we have more in common with China on Iran than we disagree on,” U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said earlier this month on Newsmax’s “Rob Schmitt Tonight”. “We both agree that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon.”

The Trump administration needs a history lesson: Iran has a nuclear weapons program only because China, both directly and indirectly, supplied it with what it needed to build nukes.

China first sent nuclear weapons tech to Pakistan, which then took on the role of China’s surrogate by distributing nuclear technology across the Asian landmass, including the Middle East and North Korea. The “father of Pakistan’s bomb,” Abdul Qadeer Khan, confessed to nuclear sales to Iran, among others. Iran got its first centrifuges — supersonic-speed machines that separate uranium gas into different isotopes and upgrade the potent material to weapons-grade purity — from Khan.

The breakup of Khan’s network in the first decade of this century was a setback for Chinese ambitions. China then employed two backup stratagems. First, Beijing permitted North Koreans to go to Iran, where hundreds of them worked in about 10 nuclear weapons and missile facilities. There were so many scientists, specialists and technicians that they took over an Iranian coastal resort , according to Henry Sokolski of the Nonproliferation Policy Education Center.

The North Koreans also sold Iran material for bomb cores, perhaps even weapons-grade uranium. The Telegraph reported that in 2002, a barrel of North Korean uranium cracked open and contaminated the tarmac of the new Tehran airport.

In October 2012, Iran began stationing personnel at a military base in North Korea, in a mountainous area close to the Chinese border. The Iranians, from the Ministry of Defense and associated firms, were reportedly working on both missile and nuclear weapons programs.

Pyongyang’s weapons sales were substantial. In 2011, Larry Niksch of the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that North Korea’s proceeds from this trade were “between $1.5 billion and $2.0 billion annually.” A portion of this amount was related to Tehran’s nuclear weapons effort.

Iran bought a lot with its money. Mohsen Fakhrizadeh, thought to be Tehran’s chief nuclear scientist, was almost certainly in North Korea at Punggye-ri in February 2011 to witness Pyongyang’s third atomic test . Reports put Iranian technicians on hand at the site for the first two detonations as well.

What were China’s ties to the North Korea-Iran trade? China helped Pyongyang build its bomb and tightly controlled the Kim regime, especially after Moscow could no longer fund North Korea after the Soviet collapse. No surprise then that the shadowy Fakhrizadeh was reported to have traveled through China on his way to North Korea to observe the nation’s third test, and China was almost certainly used as a transit point for travel to the other two North Korean detonations.

China’s second post-Khan stratagem was to take over Pakistan’s role directly. As the Khan network was being dismantled, Beijing supplemented the indirect routes through Pakistan and North Korea by stepping up direct transfers of materials and equipment to Tehran. It appears that China was smuggling parts to Iran since at least the late 1990s .

In November 2003, for instance, the staff of the International Atomic Energy Agency had fingered China as one of the sources of equipment used in Iran’s nuclear weapons program. Chinese nuclear specialists were toiling away in Iran in the fall of 2003, according to Iran analyst Michael Ledeen.

The National Council of Resistance of Iran, the dissident group that in 2002 disclosed the heavy-water production facility at Arak and the underground uranium-enrichment plant in Natanz, charged in September 2005 that China had been secretly selling centrifuges to Iran since 2003.

The group also said that the Chinese in 2004 had surreptitiously sent Iran beryllium , a metal used in neutron initiators to trigger nuclear weapons. Due to the covert nature of the transfers, it is highly unlikely that Iran bought the material for peaceful purposes. The allegation is consistent with other reports about Iran’s covert attempts to source beryllium at that time.

In July 2007, the Wall Street Journal reported that the State Department had lodged formal protests with Beijing about Chinese companies, in violation of the first two Security Council resolutions on Iran, exporting items that could help Tehran build nukes.

In March 2011, Malaysian police in Port Klang seized two containers from a ship en route to Iran from China. Authorities suspected that items labeled “goods used for liquid mixing or storage for pharmaceutical or chemical or food industry” were actually parts for nuclear warheads.

Officials in Asia confiscated shipments of equipment and materials sold by Chinese state enterprises to Iranian companies regularly. Chinese entities have been implicated in transfers of maraging steel , ring-shaped magnets and valves and vacuum gauges , all apparently for use in Iran’s atom bomb effort.

Secretary Bessent, it is China that has made Iran dangerous.

articles.body:
California, the largest producer of agricultural goods in the U.S., will begin tracking the use of “forever chemicals” in agricultural pesticides under a new law.

Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) on Sunday signed into law A.B. 1603, which requires the California Department of Pesticide Regulation to identify pesticides containing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, known as PFAS, in the state’s public pesticide database.

The new requirements could provide environmental and health officials with more information about the use of PFAS on California farmland. The state produces nearly half of the nation’s vegetables and more than three-quarters of fruits and nuts grown on domestic soil.

“As a father, I don’t want my kids eating strawberries contaminated with chemicals that will stay in their bodies for decades,” Assemblymember Nick Schultz (D), who authored the bill, said in a press release. “I’m thankful Governor Newsom agrees that families deserve to know what’s being sprayed on their food.”

PFAS are a large class of synthetic chemicals commonly called “forever chemicals” because of how slowly they break down in the environment and in the human body. They can be found throughout the environment and in manmade commercial products, including Teflon cookware, rain jackets and fast food wrappers.

Certain PFAS have been linked to health problems, including some cancers, high cholesterol and dire effects on the immune system.

An earlier version of the bill would have barred California regulators from approving new pesticides containing PFAS, drawing opposition from agricultural groups.

Lawmakers ultimately removed the proposed prohibition and instead required the state to collect and disclose information about PFAS pesticide use.

Schultz said the law is “a vital step toward ensuring California’s agricultural legacy is defined by health and innovation. Tracking and monitoring is the crucial first step.”

“You can’t fix what you can’t see,” he continued.

articles.title: Trump posts letter with ‘Unites States’ typo after AI meeting with tech CEOs
articles.summary: The letter detailing President Trump’s pact with key AI leaders posted Tuesday following his meeting with technology leaders contains a typo, misspelling his title as “President of the Unites States.” The letter, which Trump posted on Truth Social, outlined the voluntary agreement to implement certain guardrails following several high-profile cybersecurity incidents where AI chatbots escaped…
articles.body:
The letter detailing President Trump’s pact with key AI leaders posted Tuesday following his meeting with technology leaders contains a typo, misspelling his title as “President of the Unites States.”

The letter, which Trump posted on Truth Social , outlined the voluntary agreement to implement certain guardrails following several high-profile cybersecurity incidents where AI chatbots escaped testing environments and attacked databases from other companies.

The White House posted the same pledge on the social platform X Wednesday morning, which also contained the typo in Trump’s title.

The self-policing agreement was signed by Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI CEO Elon Musk and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Trump told reporters on the White House North Lawn the pledge acts “almost like a constitution” and is “morally binding,” adding “there’s going to be a tremendous self-policing aspect.” He also said they are considering forming a committee that can “watch over the whole entity.”

Zuckerberg described the agreement as giving “the American people and our customers confidence that the technology works in the way that we intend.”

The pledge also featured the president’s renaming of artificial intelligence to “super intelligence” across the executive branch.

He announced the name change during his speech at the United Nations General Assembly earlier this month and stated that all U.S. documents would use “super intelligence” or “SI” instead.

The pledge and meeting come after OpenAI revealed in July that some of its AI agents went rogue and hacked into the systems of technology startup Hugging Face. Anthropic similarly said at the time its Claude models unlawfully accessed the systems of three organizations during cybersecurity testing.

The White House did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment about the typo.

articles.title: Mamdani’s antisemitism plan draws criticism as rabbis say it avoids key driver of hate
articles.summary: Three leading rabbis across Manhattan say they were never consulted on NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's antisemitism plan or how funding was allocated.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a multimillion-dollar strategy to combat antisemitism, drawing criticism from prominent Jewish leaders who described the announcement as an attempt to deflect attention from the mayor’s own rhetoric while avoiding one of the defining sources of modern anti-Jewish hostility: the demonization of Israel and Zionism. Mamdani announced what his administration called the nation’s first municipal strategy dedicated to combating antisemitism, declaring that Jewish New Yorkers "should feel cherished and celebrated in the most Jewish city in America." The mayor cited New York Police Department statistics showing that although Jewish residents constitute approximately 12% of the city’s population, antisemitic incidents account for more than half of its confirmed hate crimes. EXCLUSIVE: ISRAELI PRESIDENT HERZOG BLASTS MAMDANI, PRAISES TRUMP, SOUNDS ALARM ON IRAN "This is not only unacceptable, it’s something we all have an obligation to change," Mamdani said. "And City Hall will lead the way." His administration said it is increasing hate crime prevention funding by $26 million, an increase of more than 800% from the previous year. The plan includes $6.4 million for community organizations working to prevent hate violence and would restart an interagency security and infrastructure initiative disbanded in 2024. The city also pledged $2 million for the Queens Holocaust Memorial Garden and $2.5 million for the Brooklyn Center for New Jewish Culture, alongside expanded education, reporting resources and security support for Jewish institutions. The way that money would be distributed also drew scrutiny. Rabbi Chaim Steinmetz, senior rabbi of Congregation Kehilath Jeshurun on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, said that only $1 million is dedicated specifically to security while millions more would be directed through community initiatives. MAMDANI IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER FIRST VETO DERAILS BIPARTISAN EFFORT TO COMBAT ANTISEMITISM: 'DISAPPOINTED' "All of this money is pure pork barrel politics," Steinmetz told Fox News Digital. "Outside of a million dollars in security, it is all being spent on community initiatives that will reward his supporters." The Jewish leaders who spoke with Fox News Digital welcomed the security investments but argued that physical protection alone cannot address an environment in which Jews increasingly feel pressured to distance themselves from Israel. From Manhattan’s East Side to its West Side, three prominent rabbis shared another concern: Not one had been contacted by the mayor or his administration while the strategy was being developed, despite collectively leading some of the borough’s largest Jewish congregations. Those concerns raise basic questions about how the strategy was constructed: which Jewish leaders and institutions helped shape it, how did the administration decide where the funding would go, and how were organizations selected to receive it? Fox News Digital asked those questions, along with Steinmetz’s criticism of the funding process, to the mayor’s office but had not received a response at the time of publication. The mayor's strategy acknowledges rising antisemitism since Oct. 7 and expands Holocaust education, but does not directly address the hostility Jewish students have experienced on college campuses or examine when anti-Israel activism crosses into antisemitic harassment and intimidation. The three rabbis interviewed by Fox News Digital identified that omission as a significant weakness in the city’s strategy. Rabbi Ammiel Hirsch, senior rabbi of Stephen Wise Free Synagogue in Manhattan and president of the New York Board of Rabbis, said the plan omits what he considers the central driver of contemporary antisemitism. CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS "If the purpose here is to combat and reduce antisemitism, the plan omits the central driver of contemporary antisemitism, which is an obsessive loathing of Israel," Hirsch told Fox News Digital. That hostility, he said, is directed "not only" toward the state of Israel but toward "the Zionist idea, the right of Israel to exist, the right of the Jewish people to self-determination in the land of Israel." "To write a 30-page report and never mention the state of Israel, let alone address the vicious anti-Zionism, partially fomented by the mayor himself, is evading the issue," Hirsch said. "It’s not dealing head-on with the issue itself." ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS Hirsch welcomed the additional security funding, while emphasizing that Jewish institutions must routinely absorb expenses other communities do not face. "The security obligations in every Jewish institution in the city are, in effect, an additional surtax on New York Jews that nobody else pays," he said. "And so any funds for security are welcome." He also supported educational initiatives and Holocaust museum visits but said the city must teach more than the history of Jewish persecution. "What I would like to see is a focus in New York public schools on the nexus, the connection between anti-Zionism and antisemitism," Hirsch said. "One of the key lessons from the Holocaust," he added, is that "Jewish self-determination and Jewish empowerment are the answer to Jewish powerlessness that gave rise to centuries of antisemitism that culminated in genocide." Steinmetz also said the mayor is using the strategy to avoid examining the consequences of his own language. "Rather than taking responsibility for combating antisemitism, Mamdani is using this plan to deflect attention from himself," Steinmetz said. "His rhetoric has been reckless." SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER Steinmetz said statistics measuring physical crimes capture only part of what Jewish New Yorkers experience. "Far more common is the nasty look and whispered insult," he said. "You cannot talk about a trip to Israel at the water cooler. Jews feel like they have to hide parts of themselves to be accepted." The mayor has long been an outspoken critic of the Israeli government and has faced scrutiny from Jewish leaders over his descriptions of Israel, Zionism and organizations that support the Jewish state. Critics argue that separating antisemitism from anti-Zionist rhetoric ignores how Jewish identity is experienced by much of the city’s Jewish population. Rabbi Yosie Levine of The Jewish Center on Manhattan’s Upper West Side thanked the mayor for recognizing the severity of the problem but called for a corresponding change in his language. "I want to thank the mayor for his commitment to combat antisemitism," Levine told Fox News Digital. "Acknowledging the problem is an important first step." ISRAELI MEDICS TRAIN US SYNAGOGUES HOW TO RESPOND TO ATTACKS, AS HIGH HOLIDAYS APPROACH "At the same time, we would welcome an equally clear commitment to stop using rhetoric that vilifies Jewish leaders and the Jewish state," Levine continued. "When you turn Zionism into an accusation, you turn Zionists into the accused." A spokesperson for the Jewish Federations of North America, referred Fox News Digital to a joint statement issued by UJA Federation of New York and the Jewish Community Relations Council of New York. While the organizations recognized "positive elements" in the plan, including increased security funding and the expansion of established programs, they warned that it "fails to address a central issue that the mayor himself has perpetuated: rhetoric that demonizes and delegitimizes Israel inevitably leads to the targeting of Jewish New Yorkers." "Those who truly seek to address antisemitism must unequivocally reject such rhetoric and help ensure that Jewish New Yorkers are never made to feel suspect, excluded or unsafe in their own city," the statement continued. Mamdani said the administration’s efforts would ultimately benefit every community because "our safety is bound up together." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Fundamentally, what is lacking is even an acknowledgment that obsessive loathing of Israel is generating much of this antisemitism," Hirsch said. "It would have been much more mature and, frankly, much more useful to lay out that fact." "Simply to omit it and avoid it is a wasted opportunity," he concluded. "I’m disappointed in the mayor, and he should have done better."

articles.title: Medicare should help doctors prevent disease, not just pay for it
articles.summary: Rep. Gregory F. Murphy proposed that Medicare Advantage plans should be allowed to provide nutritious food as a targeted clinical intervention to help seniors manage chronic diseases and prevent costly hospitalizations.
articles.body:
As a physician, I have spent my career treating patients with chronic diseases. One lesson becomes obvious very quickly: preventing a patient from getting sicker is always better than treating them after their health has deteriorated.

Unfortunately, Medicare’s current rules have it backwards.

Today, more than 35 million Americans are enrolled in Medicare Advantage, and more than 85 percent have at least two chronic diseases. Many of these conditions are diet-related and can be improved with nutrition-based clinical interventions. Research shows that targeted nutrition can improve health outcomes and reduce costly hospitalizations.

Doctors know this. Patients know this. Medicare policy hasn’t caught up.

Under current rules, Medicare Advantage plans can provide healthy food benefits to a narrow subset of chronically ill seniors, but generally only after they incur high costs, including being at significant risk for hospitalization and requiring intensive care management.

A physician may know that better nutrition could help a patient control his diabetes or manage her heart disease. But Medicare effectively says: wait until that patient gets sicker and more expensive to treat before making that tool available.

Meanwhile, Medicare Advantage plans can cover “fitness benefits” like bowling balls, wi-fi, and ski passes, from Day One.

Yes, you read that correctly. Under Medicare’s rules, it’s easier to cover a bowling ball than healthy food prescribed by a doctor to manage chronic disease.

We can fix this today, without an act of Congress, without creating a new entitlement, and without spending another taxpayer dollar.

I recently led a letter asking Medicare administrator Mehmet Oz to recognize healthy food as a “primarily health related” supplemental benefit for qualifying Medicare Advantage patients. This common-sense change would allow plans to make clinically appropriate nutrition available earlier in a patient’s care, when it may actually prevent more serious and expensive complications.

This is not food assistance or an unrestricted grocery benefit. It is a targeted clinical intervention for patients with chronic conditions, with eligible foods tied to the government’s official dietary guidelines . Most important to me as a physician, healthy food should be available to seniors when their doctor determines it is medically necessary.

If a physician knows better nutrition can help a patient manage diabetes today, why should Washington require that patient to get sicker before Medicare gives the doctor the tools to help?

There is a taxpayer argument here, too. The Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services already sends billions of taxpayer dollars to Medicare Advantage plans for supplemental benefits. This proposal doesn’t spend a dime more. It simply allows plans to put existing resources toward preventing disease rather than paying for its consequences.

For too long, our health care system has rewarded sick care rather than health care.

The MAHA agenda of the Trump administration and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is changing that paradigm by addressing chronic disease and putting prevention first. CMS has an opportunity to turn that principle into action for millions of American seniors.

For the first time in Medicare’s history, we can formally recognize healthy food as a targeted clinical intervention to prevent and manage chronic disease.

We don’t need a new government program. We don’t need billions in new spending. We just need Medicare’s rules to catch up with the evidence and give doctors the ability to intervene before their patients end up in the hospital.

That’s better medicine, better stewardship of taxpayer dollars and a healthier Medicare program.

Gregory F. Murphy, M.D., represents North Carolina’s 3rd District in the U.S. House of Representatives.

articles.title: Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifts 11 House seats in Democrats’ favor
articles.summary: Election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball on Tuesday shifted 11 House seats toward Democrats as the country inches closer to the November midterm elections. The forecaster’s report shifted the race for Virginia’s 1st Congressional District, led by Rep. Rob Wittman (R-Va.), from leaning Republican to a toss-up. Wittman is considered a strong incumbent, with his Democratic…
articles.body:
Election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball on Tuesday shifted 11 House seats toward Democrats as the country inches closer to the November midterm elections.

The forecaster’s report shifted the race for Virginia’s 1st Congressional District, led by Rep. Rob Wittman (R-Va.), from leaning Republican to a toss-up. Wittman is considered a strong incumbent, with his Democratic opponent, Henrico County attorney Shannon Taylor, behind him by 1 point.

“If Taylor ends up beating Wittman, it would certainly suggest a Democratic majority larger than the narrow ones both sides have held in recent years. The district has attracted a considerable amount of Democratic outside spending so far,” Crystal Ball associate editor J. Miles Coleman wrote.

The races for Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District, led by Rep. Jen Kiggans (R), and Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District, held by Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R), moved from being toss-ups to leaning Democratic. Kiggans leads one of the most evenly split districts in the 2024 election, while Mackenzie faces an opponent who has raised more money and campaigned with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D).

Coleman shifted the races in North Carolina’s 3rd Congressional District, led by Rep. Greg Murphy (R), and Ohio’s 15th Congressional District, led by Rep. Mike Carey (R), from being safe GOP districts to “likely Republican.”

Murphy’s redrawn district, referred to by opponents as a “dummymander,” could be difficult for Democrats to claim. Coleman wrote that Murphy’s opponent, former state Rep. Raymond Smith (D), has attracted outside support and used more than $300,000 in outside spending against Murphy.

Carey has also faced more outside spending and is narrowly behind Democrat Don Leonard, according to the Democrat-aligned House Majority PAC. Coleman warned to “take the publicly released internals with a grain of salt.”

Five districts shifted from “likely Republican” to leaning Republican. Those districts consist of Missouri’s 2nd Congressional District, held by Rep. Ann Wagner (R); Rep. John McGuire’s (R) 5th Congressional District in Virginia; and the open seats for Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, Maine’s 2nd Congressional District and Montana’s 1st Congressional District.

California’s 45th Congressional District shifted from leaning Democratic to “likely Democratic.” Rep. Derek Tran (D-Calif.) is seen as the clear favorite after a close victory in 2024 and after he won 54 percent of the vote in the June primary.

Coleman said Tran has “more of a cushion” due to the Golden State’s passage of Proposition 50, which redrew the state’s congressional map to give Democrats a potential chance at winning up to 5 seats in November.

Coleman said Republicans had a “tough month” as Democrats expanded their lead on the House ballot, citing Emerson College’s poll last week showing 78 percent of Democrats being excited to vote compared with 66 percent of Republican voters.

“And — getting more to the Green Day pun that we led with — many pollsters have consistently shown that Democrats are just more enthused than Republicans,” he quipped, noting the report’s title, “Will Republicans Wake Up As September Ends?”

Decision Desk HQ’s forecast projects Democrats are very likely to reclaim the House with a 75 percent probability, while Republicans have a 25 percent chance of holding their majority. It’s much narrower in the Senate, where Democrats have a 55 percent chance of taking control of the upper chamber and Republicans have a 45 percent likelihood of maintaining their majority.

articles.title: Leave your politics behind: Greenland is a historic US victory
articles.summary: The United States, Denmark, and Greenland signed a permanent agreement granting the U.S. broad military access to Greenland to bolster North Atlantic security and counter influence from Russia and China.
articles.body:
The U.S., Denmark and Greenland have signed an agreement that will be the biggest American strategic gain in the Northern Hemisphere in a generation.

The agreement has no expiration date and provides enduring military and security advantages in support of the U.S. national defense while allowing Denmark to retain its sovereignty over Greenland’s more than 825,000 square miles of territory.

Politics should not cloud this strategic victory for the U.S. which increases NATO security and builds relationships.

From basing to overflight rights, the new agreement gives the U.S. broad military access to Greenland. During the Cold War, the U.S. operated numerous installations in Greenland, but has since reduced its presence to only Pituffik Space Base . The new agreement creates opportunities for the U.S. to expand its activities at Pituffik Space Base and, subject to further agreement on the details, establish defense areas at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and Mestersvig in the East. It also sets out a process for additional defense areas and expedited review of proposed unmanned military installations.

Greenland is critical to the defense of the American homeland and the North Atlantic for two reasons. First, it sits on the western edge of the Greenland-Iceland-United Kingdom gap, a key naval chokepoint. Second, it hosts forward-based radar coverage along the shortest path that Russian ballistic missiles and long-range aircraft would take to reach the U.S.

A great-circle route from Moscow to Washington passes near Greenland’s southern tip and is roughly 4,800 miles. For comparison, an aircraft flying from Moscow to Washington by way of Paris would travel over 500 miles farther.

What’s more, Greenland’s ability to monitor satellites passing over the polar region makes it one of the most valuable pieces of terrain for American missile warning, space surveillance, and future missile-defense systems, including Golden Dome, which the agreement specifically discusses as a purpose of expanded American access.

Furthermore, melting Arctic ice is increasing seasonal access to shipping routes and formerly rugged areas where China has already asserted itself. China’s 2018 Arctic policy calls the country a “Near-Arctic State” and seeks a role in Arctic shipping, infrastructure, and resource development through what it calls a “Polar Silk Road.” Under the new agreement, American public vessels will receive undersea access within Greenland’s territorial waters, helping the U.S. and its allies patrol and monitor the Arctic as these routes become more accessible.

The agreement also limits the opportunities for China and Russia to gain a military foothold in Greenland. Non-NATO states cannot establish military installations or maintain a persistent military presence unless the parties agree. Denmark and Greenland must also screen foreign activity in sensitive sectors, including infrastructure and resource extraction for threats to national security. Those provisions matter even more if Greenland chooses independence: the agreement requires an independent Greenland to assume its obligations and remain in NATO or apply to join.

Finally, the agreement places the United States in a stronger position as Greenland’s resources and the Arctic become more important. Greenland has an estimated 1.5 million metric tons of rare-earth reserves. It also has large deposits or prospects involving copper, nickel, zinc, tungsten, uranium, graphite, platinum-group metals, gold, and iron. These resources are some of important components of weapons, aircraft, radar, electronics, batteries, motors, and advanced manufacturing.

The broader West Greenland-East Canada geological province is estimated to contain 7.8 billion barrels of undiscovered, technically recoverable oil and 91.9 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. Although the agreement does not outright give the U.S. ownership of Greenland’s mineral resources or automatic extraction rights, it does help prevent American competitors, like China and Russia, from getting control of sensitive resource sectors and creates better conditions for future American and allied investment.

The U.S. did not seize or purchase Greenland. It secured broad military access, strengthened the defense of North America, and placed enduring restrictions on non-NATO countries establishing a military foothold on the island. The people of Greenland retain the right to decide their political future, while the agreement is designed to preserve American access if they choose independence. Whatever one thinks of the politics that led here, those are substantial gains and a strategic U.S. victory.

John Spencer is the chair of War Studies at the Madison Policy Forum, where Frank Viola is a fellow.

(AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson, File)

President Trump will host a Hispanic Heritage Month celebration Wednesday at the White House, as both the GOP and Democrats seek to appeal to Hispanic voters with the midterms just more than a month away.

Democrats have shown signs of making gains with the voting bloc in key battleground districts during the primaries, after Trump made significant inroads with Hispanic voters in 2024.

Republicans, meanwhile, are looking to hold on to those gains. Rep. María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) said recently that Hispanic voters remain receptive to Trump despite his falling approval numbers , affordability concerns and frustrations over his immigration agenda .

The president marked Hispanic Heritage Month by praising Hispanic Americans’ contributions to the country and highlighting what he described as their commitment to “faith, family, and freedom.” He also used the message to tout his administration’s economic gains — including tax breaks on tips and overtime and an expanded child tax credit .

The event is scheduled to begin at 1 p.m. EDT.

articles.title: Sarah Huckabee Sanders bombs with anti-welfare ad starring young white man
articles.summary: Sarah Huckabee Sanders is the Republican governor of Arkansas, and she’s currently running for a second term. As former press secretary to President Trump, she’s a popular figure within MAGA, and of course, Arkansas is a very red state. And yet she just put out an anti-welfare ad that’s bombing — with conservatives, because of…
articles.body:
Sarah Huckabee Sanders is the Republican governor of Arkansas, and she’s currently running for a second term. As former press secretary to President Trump, she’s a popular figure within MAGA, and of course, Arkansas is a very red state. And yet she just put out an anti-welfare ad that’s bombing — with conservatives, because of who is portrayed in it.

You might think conservatives would be nodding their head in agreement, but no. They’re furious that Huckabee Sanders settled on Brad, a 20-something white guy, as the villain here. Many accounts pointed that 20-something white guys are not the demographic most likely to be on welfare, and so in their view, the ad is poking fun at the wrong target.

Kangnin Lee wrote on X : “Young right-wing Christian American gamers are some of the most patriotic people in society. This is tonedeaf and the only reason you did this was because they’re the easiest demographic to put down.”

And Jenna Ellis wrote : “Who advised Sarah this was a good idea?! Some young white men may still live on their parents’ welfare, but very few live on government welfare. Those are two completely different issues. Don’t make the young white male (a voting demo the GOP needs) the enemy here.”

For my part, I say let’s take race out of it entirely. Personally, I’m getting sick of hearing that the problem in our society is too many lazy young people relying on welfare. It’s not true! By far, the biggest welfare expenditure in the country is Medicare, and the beneficiaries of it are disproportionately the elderly, who already hold most of the wealth in society. It’s socialism for the rich, and the rest of us are paying for it.

The GOP needs to understand that young people, by some measures, have it a lot harder than they used to. Regulations that constrain the building of new houses have made it harder for young people to become homeowners. Policy choices have also made child care and education more expensive. At the same time, young people have to pay a huge share of their income to support social programs that mostly benefit their grandparents. They’re not lazing about at home playing video games — they’re working hard to keep ahead of the rent bill, the child care bill, and worst of all, the tax bill.

I think that’s really why this ad came across as tone deaf. Yes, of course the governor is right, people who receive welfare benefits like food stamps should absolutely be working or actively seeking employment. I don’t think anyone in the GOP disagrees with that. In fact, there are probably a lot of conservatives and libertarians who would be OK with dramatically reducing or eliminating these programs entirely.

But SNAP costs $100 billion a year. Medicare costs more than a trillion dollars a year, and Social Security is another $1.6 trillion. It’s not young white guys who love video games living it up as welfare queens — it’s not young people at all. It’s the people who rigged the system so that you make, they take, and live it up, even though they’ve had decades to make a lot more money.

Doesn’t seem fair to me, but older Americans are reliable voters, and so the governor is eager to cater to their sense of fairness.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Democrats block bill restricting lawmakers from trading stocks
articles.summary: Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked a bill sponsored by vulnerable GOP incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts (Neb.) to restrict members of Congress from buying new stocks of publicly traded companies, arguing the legislation didn’t go far enough to crack down on possible corruption. The Stop Insider Trading Act failed by a vote of 53-47. No Democrat…
articles.body:
Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked a bill sponsored by vulnerable GOP incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts (Neb.) to restrict members of Congress from buying new stocks of publicly traded companies, arguing the legislation didn’t go far enough to crack down on possible corruption.

The Stop Insider Trading Act failed by a vote of 53-47. No Democrat voted in support of the measure.

It needed 60 votes to advance on the Senate floor.

Ricketts, who is facing a competitive race in Nebraska, argued before the vote that his bill would “ban congressional insider trading” and touted it as a “commonsense” reform that “we need to pass.”

It passed the House in July by a vote of 232-198 with the support of 13 Democrats.

“Congress’s approval rating is only 15 percent. Why do Americans have such a lack of faith in our institutions? Well, in part, because of what has happened with trading in the Congress,” Ricketts said on the Senate floor before the vote.

Ricketts has been accused by his campaign opponent, independent Dan Osborn, of profiting handsomely from his stock portfolio during his time in the Senate.

Osborne slammed Ricketts for making an estimated $10 million in market gains in April of last year, when stocks bounced back after President Trump eased off of his sweeping “Liberation Day” tariffs.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) panned Ricketts’s proposal as a “feeble” attempt at reform that would still allow lawmakers to engage in profitable transactions.

“Only Senate Republicans would dare call a bill that permits members of Congress to continue to own, sell and in some instances buy stocks a stock-trading ban. They can’t be serious. The Republican bill is a permission slip for corruption, not a stock-trading ban,” Schumer declared on the Senate floor.

The legislation would have banned lawmakers from buying new stocks in publicly traded companies and would have required them to provide advance notice of plans to sell stocks.

But the legislation would have allowed lawmakers to keep the stocks they already own and to buy private stocks.

Schumer argued that the Senate Homeland Security Committee last year approved a stronger bipartisan bill.

He said House Republicans watered it down before passing it over the summer and added a “poison pill” by adding a provision that would require people to present valid voter identification when voting.

“Republicans want to explicitly allow members to continue trading stocks in privately held companies, including companies the members oversee, a formula for disaster and corruption,” he said.

Schumer criticized the legislation on Tuesday for not including a ban on President Trump trading stocks, noting that Trump and his money managers executed approximately 28,700 trades between January 2025 and June 2026, according to a Bloomberg analysis.

Democrats have attacked Sen. Dan Sullivan (R), who faces a tough race in Alaska, for expanding his net worth through stock trades during his time in the Senate.

Senate Democrats this month accused Sullivan of tripling his wealth while in office and pointed to reporting that he sold off shares after attending a closed-door meeting before those stocks dipped.

WinSenate, a super PAC aligned with Senate Democratic leadership, has aired a new ad featuring a line cook and bartender from Homer, Alaska, who criticizes Sullivan for having “nearly quadrupled his net worth” and “cutting healthcare for Alaskans” while in Congress.

Wednesday’s vote marked the latest instance of a proposal to limit stock trading by members of Congress failing on the Senate floor.

In June, Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) objected to a unanimous consent request by Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) to ban senators from buying or selling stocks and cryptocurrency.

In July, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) objected to a request by Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) to pass the bipartisan HONEST Act, which would have prohibited the president, vice president and members of Congress from owning, acquiring or selling individual stocks and digital assets.

Moreno at the time dismissed the effort as a “publicity show.”

articles.summary: Plus: 🔦Schmitt stays in the spotlight {beacon} It’s Wednesday, and the Senate is busy. In today’s issue: Latest on Ratepayer Protection Act Schmitt stays in the limelight Iran targets U.S. midterms Ken Griffin’s $3 billion donation Programming note: We’re Joshua Feldstein and Abigail Walker, filling in for Cate today. Please send us your…
articles.body:
Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Abigail Walker, filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and awalker@thehill.com.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) could go 0 for 2 on major Senate legislative items on Wednesday.

Senators began a three-part vote-series at 11:30, with Thune moving to advance the Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to ensure data centers don’t increase consumer energy costs; the Stop Insider Trading Act, a congressional stock trading ban passed by the House in July; and advancing the nomination of Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling to the permanent post.

Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) views the Ratepayer Protection Act as “ a political lifeline ” for its sponsor, Sen. Jon Husted ( R-Ohio), who’s locked in a tough midterm race — likely dooming its chances of getting the 60 votes needed.

Husted, along with Sens. Dan Sullivan (Alaska), Pete Ricketts (Neb.) and Roger Marshall (Kan.)—all running for reelection—are looking increasingly vulnerable in states that went safely for Trump two years ago.

An AARP poll released earlier this month found Sullivan trailing former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) by 5 percentage points. The Bowling Green State University (BGSU) survey had Husted 3 points behind his Democratic opponent, former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown .

As The Hill’s Alexander Bolton points out : “In Ohio — where 75 percent of voters oppose the construction of data centers in their communities, according to one recent poll — Democratic Senate candidate Brown has tagged Husted as ‘the face of data centers in Ohio.'”

No deal: Democrats were set to sink the Stop Insider Trading Act, which includes a stock-trading ban but also elements of the SAVE America election reform package, which are a non-starter for most Democrats.

The Stop Insider Trading Act is the latest attempt to put limits on how lawmakers and members of their family can buy and trade stocks — a major topic of conversation due to the rise in prediction markets.

The act was passed by the House in July.

The deal with data centers: The Ratepayer Protection Act seeks to address data centers’ electricity costs, but Democrats say it doesn’t go far enough.

With Schumer speaking out against the proposal, it appears unlikely to get the 60 votes needed to advance in the upper chamber.

The vote could come anytime this afternoon.

Republicans accuse Schumer of playing politics with a popular bill, pointing to its 417-3 passage in the House.

“The Ratepayer Protection Act is such a no brainer that almost the most conservative and the most liberal representatives all agreed it was a good policy,” Husted said on the Senate floor.

“If Democrats block this bill, they will prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that they do not care about affordability and that they will not do anything to take action to help.”

Not buying it : Sen. Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.) told The Hill on Tuesday that she’d vote against the data center bill, writing it off as a ploy to boost support for Husted.

“This bill … has no teeth,” she said. “This is just a pivot,” Rosen said.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), who is running for Senate in the Lone Star State, said he thinks the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) midterm convention damaged his campaign .

“So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good,” he said in an audio clip, which was shared by The New York Times .

The convention, dubbed “Trump-a-palooza” and hosted in Dallas, intended to energize Republicans. In one late-night speech, Trump encouraged voters to support Paxton while also criticizing the attorney general’s appearance and demeanor.

Nonsense? Paxton’s senior adviser Nick Maddux told the Times that “this is more manipulated nonsense from The New York Times to create a story that doesn’t exist.”

Paxton’s remarks, which the outlet says were made at a private fundraiser in Washington, D.C., add heat to an already tense Texas Senate race.

His opponent, Democrat James Talarico, is leading by 2 points in polls, according to latest averages from Decision Desk HQ .

Democratic lawmakers are lining up to criticize Sen. Eric Schmitt’s (R-Mo.) sports team mix-up during former special counsel Jack Smith’s hearing.

On Tuesday, Schmitt asked Smith if he had attended a February 2024 NBA game between the Atlanta Hawks and Golden State Warriors in Atlanta, but after Smith’s response, it appeared that Schmitt confused the Hawks with the Iowa Hawkeyes, whose star Caitlin Clark played in College Park, Md. on that date.

Schmitt was trying to prove that Smith was in Atlanta around the time of key developments in the election fraud case brought by Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis .

Raskin’s wrath: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, said Schmitt “basically disgraced himself and identified himself with this ridiculous little stunt where he thought he was going to perform some major service to Donald Trump.”

“And he doesn’t even understand how much that he’s utterly humiliated himself in the eyes of the country,” Raskin told CNN’s Erin Burnett in a conversation Tuesday night.

Members of the Senate Judiciary Committee such as Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif) and Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) accused Schmitt of attempting to create a false narrative about Smith.

“It looked like he had text messages suggesting that Jack Smith was at some sporting event he wasn’t at, and he hoped to catch Jack Smith in some false statement,” Schiff said. “It turns out the only thing false was the presentation.”

Just doing my job: Schmitt responded to his mistake by saying that his job “is to ask questions, and his job is to answer the questions.”

“We had information, of course, about him being at a basketball game. The only NBA game going on that night was in Atlanta on Feb. 2 of 2024. His team had talked about that. He answered the question,” Smith told Nexstar affiliate KTVI St. Louis on Tuesday.

Imperfect timing: According to an Axios report that came out hours before Schmitt’s factual flub during Smith’s hearing, he was a possible contender to be a running mate to Vice President Vance if he runs in 2028.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) signed a state ban into law Tuesday that would bar law enforcement from using electric shock gloves.

The ban will go into place next year and last through 2030, impacting local, state and federal law enforcement officers across the state.

According to The Hill’s Sarah Davis , the ban also requires the California Department of Justice to complete a safety study on the devices.

Sparking controversy: In August, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) announced that they received a $17 million contract to purchase 6,000 pairs of the gloves.

Democrats on the House Committee on Homeland Security expressed their opposition to the gloves, writing in a statement that they “have many questions about ICE’s nearly $17 million contract for a device that is likely to be incorrectly used or abused by officers and agents.”

Additional oversight: On top of Newsom’s shock glove ban, he also signed legislation that looks to increase oversight at immigration detention facilities.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesperson Gen. Hossein Mohebbi called on Americans to vote against Trump in November’s midterm elections to change U.S. policy towards Iran.

“You are the ones who empower, with your votes, the government and allow it to do what it does,” Mohebbi said in a 25-page letter obtained by the Times of Israel.

“Although American politicians often win your votes through deception and false promises, as Trump did, you can change the makeup of the government if you apply the criteria for good leadership in choosing the people you vote into office,” he continued.

Take it to the streets: According to the Associated Press, Mohebbi said Americans should rally against Trump and accused the U.S. of attempting to turn Iran “back into a colony” by focusing on their nuclear program.

Ken Griffin , the CEO and founder of Citadel Advisors LLC, is donating $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon University, the largest individual gift in higher education history and the largest donation made by a hedge fund manager.

A federal appeals court paused the execution to Christa Pike Wednesday, around an hour before it was set to happen. Pike was set to be executed by a lethal injection at 10 a.m. local time in Nashville and would have been the first women in the state to be executed in 200 years.

According to the Associated Press and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , a pilot stabbed another pilot and then reportedly tried to crash a FlyDubai plane carrying Israeli passengers Wednesday. The plane was heading from Dubai to Tel Aviv and was forced to land at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.

Trump’s nominee for U.S. surgeon general, Nicole Saphier , advanced through the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee on Wednesday by a 12-11 vote.

articles.title: Congressional investigations are coming soon — prepare your company now
articles.summary: As Democrats potentially gain control of Congress next year, companies are advised to prepare for an aggressive wave of oversight and investigations targeting politically sensitive sectors.
articles.body:
If next year begins with Democrats in control of one or both chambers of Congress, a new cohort of committee chairs will be inheriting gavels — and they’re already mapping out an aggressive oversight and investigations agenda. Companies shouldn’t assume the spotlight will stay on the administration. Don’t wait for the first letter from Capitol Hill to arrive. The time to prepare is now.

White House and agency oversight will undoubtedly be a priority for Democrats, but it’s likely to be slow and litigious. The administration has signaled that it will aggressively resist congressional requests and subpoenas, most recently in an opinion published by the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel that is certain to complicate battles over executive privilege.

The private sector, by contrast, will be an easier target: faster to produce documents, easier to haul in front of cameras, and often sitting on records a committee needs to build its story. Companies located in politically salient sectors — artificial intelligence, pharma, energy, media, financial services, and any company that cut a high-profile deal with this administration — could see letters arriving as soon as January.

Investigations are likely to come from all corners of Capitol Hill. Judiciary, Oversight and Energy and Commerce will drive some of the splashiest headlines, but they won’t be alone. Many other committee chairs will set aside a gridlocked legislative agenda to prioritize oversight, hire new investigative staff, and flex their jurisdictional muscles in new ways.

Companies should treat the next few months as an opportunity to get ready.

The instinct to route a congressional letter solely to the litigation team is understandable but often wrong. Congressional investigations run on a fundamentally different logic than civil litigation or regulatory enforcement. A committee’s first letter may appear voluntary, but it often opens a negotiation over scope, timing, process and public narrative. The response can determine whether the matter stays with staff or escalates into subpoenas, hearings and executive testimony.

There is no judge overseeing the process. A committee largely decides for itself what is relevant to a “legislative purpose,” a standard that courts have read broadly. There is no neutral arbiter, ordinary discovery schedule, or proportionality rule to rely on. That makes the first negotiation with staff critical.

Voluntary cooperation is a strategic choice. Most committees prefer negotiated compliance to subpoenas. The way a company handles the first informal request can shape what follows, including whether a subpoena comes at all.

Privilege is not a guaranteed shield. Companies often assume attorney-client and work-product protections operate in Congress the way they do in court. They do not. Committees have long taken the position that common-law privileges are recognized only at the committee’s discretion, based on the committee’s assessment of its need for the information and the potential injury from disclosure. In practice, protecting privileged material usually depends less on winning a legal ruling than on negotiating accommodations with committee staff.

The press headline is often the real sanction. Contempt referrals and civil enforcement are serious, but in reality they are often slow, uncertain, and shaped by political will, a limited congressional calendar, and (non-)cooperation from the administration. The more immediate risk is that the company becomes the story. In congressional oversight, a legally defensible position can still be a reputational mistake.

Companies should take seven steps between now and January to prepare for the coming investigations.

Map political exposure, not just legal exposure.Identify where the business touches politically salient issues — not just where it faces legal exposure — including contracts, settlements, regulatory approvals, consumer complaints, workforce issues, public controversies, or sectors already drawing Capitol Hill letters. Companies should also monitor the “fire alarms” that often trigger oversight, including investigative reporting, whistleblower complaints, Inspector General reports, Government Accountability Office findings, advocacy campaigns, state enforcement actions, and viral controversies.

Extend preservation protocols to congressional risk. Many companies’ litigation-hold triggers are keyed to filed or reasonably anticipated lawsuits. A congressional inquiry has different triggers — a public letter, a press report naming your company, a committee announcement — and preservation protocols should catch them.

Build an internal escalation path before you need it. Decide now who gets looped in when Congress calls. That could include team members from legal, government affairs, communications, business leadership and the board.

Treat minority oversight as real oversight. Minority members may not control subpoenas, but they can send letters, build public records, coordinate with watchdogs, elevate whistleblower claims, request work by inspectors general and the Government Accountability Office, and tee up issues for Day One action if control changes. Democrats’ voluntary letters now are a roadmap for potential subpoenas next year.

Pressure test your voluntary-cooperation posture. Decide in advance how the company will approach informal requests, including how to maintain constructive staff relationships while narrowing overbroad demands.

Revisit privilege. Companies should think now about which categories of documents they would fight hardest to protect, and build that judgment into their document review protocols before an inquiry forces the question under deadline pressure.

Retain outside counsel with congressional experience. Congressional investigations are not just another species of litigation, and the learning curve is steep once a committee letter has arrived. Counsel who have worked with or inside congressional committees can help anticipate how staff are likely to frame the request, which accommodations are realistic, when voluntary cooperation is strategically useful, and when a firmer line is warranted. Experienced counsel can also coordinate legal, government affairs, communications, and board-facing responses before the company is reacting under pressure.

Most companies already have the underlying muscle for investigations: custodian identification, preservation technology, cross-functional coordination — the same infrastructure that runs a litigation hold. What’s often missing is the congressional-specific playbook layered on top of it.

The gavels may not change hands until January, but the window to prepare is starting to close.

Sandeep Prasanna is counsel at Miller and Chevalier Chartered. He previously held senior House and Senate staff roles and managed congressional oversight at the Department of Justice.

articles.title: Watch live: Senate panel weighs national security risks of rogue AI
articles.summary: Industry experts on Wednesday will face questioning from members of a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee panel about the national security risks posed by rogue AI. The hearing will focus on how autonomous AI agents — including OpenAI’s model that unsuccessfully attempted to breach federal agency websites — could be used to launch…
articles.body:
Industry experts on Wednesday will face questioning from members of a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee panel about the national security risks posed by rogue AI .

The hearing will focus on how autonomous AI agents — including OpenAI’s model that unsuccessfully attempted to breach federal agency websites — could be used to launch cyberattacks, target critical infrastructure or carry out other harmful actions with limited human oversight. The subcommittee is led by Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Andy Kim (D-N.J.).

Concerns over rapidly advancing AI have grown in recent weeks, as industry leaders sound alarms about the lack of guardrails . President Trump, who on Tuesday ordered the federal government to begin referring to the tech as “super intelligence,” has resisted calls for sweeping federal regulations.

The president also welcomed several tech CEOs to the White House on Tuesday, including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, to sign a voluntary accord aimed at establishing self-policing when it comes to the tech.

The event is scheduled to begin at 2:30 p.m. EDT.

articles.title: JMSN lawyers demand White House drop R&B artist’s song from controversial Trump ad
articles.summary: The music artist behind a song included in a government-funded commercial highlighting President Trump’s political agenda has sent a cease-and-desist letter to the White House. JMSN’s song “Love Me” is featured prominently in the advertisement that recently aired on TV and was posted to the White House’s YouTube page in early September. In the 30-second…
articles.body:
The music artist behind a song included in a government-funded commercial highlighting President Trump’s political agenda has sent a cease-and-desist letter to the White House.

JMSN’s song “Love Me” is featured prominently in the advertisement that recently aired on TV and was posted to the White House’s YouTube pag e in early September. In the 30-second commercial — one of several ads to air in recent weeks featuring a “paid for by the U.S. government” disclaimer — rapid-fire images of Trump are shown as the 2023 tune plays in the background.

“America will never be a communist country,” the president said in the clip.

“I therefore write to demand that the government immediately cease and desist from any further use of ‘Love Me.’ I further insist that the government refrain from using any of JMSN’s music in the future,” a legal team representing JMSN, the moniker for singer Christian Berishaj, said Monday in a letter sent to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

“To be absolutely clear, JMSN does not want to be viewed as directly or indirectly affiliated with the President or his Administration,” the letter continued, before referencing a recent Instagram post from the performer.

“To anybody who has followed my career and knows what I stand for and built my career on, it should go without saying that I would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign,” JMSN wrote on Instagram .

Attorney Norm Eisen and law firm Ballard Spahr, both representing the 39-year-old singer, said the use of the song “as part of an overtly partisan, political advertisement is particularly damaging, as it could cause others to call into question JMSN’s artistic independence and integrity.”

The “unauthorized use” of the music, the letter noted, “does further harm because it associates JMSN and the song with apparent violations of federal laws prohibiting the use of taxpayer dollars for political purposes.”

The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about the cease-and-desist letter.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have criticized the government-funded ads featuring the president.

“It’s a great message, I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said Monday.

“It would not have been something that I would have done,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said.

The White House has defended the commercials as “very clearly not campaign ads” — instead calling them “a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending.”

Several entertainers have objected to Trump’s use of their songs at his campaign rallies and in videos posted to social media over the years.

Earlier this month, “Midnight Sun” singer Zara Larsson ripped the White House for using her hit song in a video posted to the White House’s TikTok account accompanied by footage of immigration arrests and deportations.

Other artists and music groups to publicly object to use of their songs by the Trump administration or his campaign include the Foo Fighters, Jack White of the White Stripes and Celine Dion.

articles.title: Why opponents mistake Flock cameras for tools of totalitarian control
articles.summary: An entrepreneur argues that opponents of Flock Safety’s automated license plate reading technology mistakenly equate the collection of data with its potential misuse, suggesting that tools should be judged by the philosophy of those who use them rather than being banned outright.
articles.body:
One issue has been uniting the left, right and libertarians : abolishing, banning and curtailing Flock cameras, an automated license plate reading system made by Flock Safety. Installed on streets and poles, they capture vehicle plates, make, model, color and unique features to log travel data into a searchable database. Police can search for a specific vehicle and see where and when it was detected, allowing investigators to trace a vehicle’s movements and develop leads in cases ranging from thefts to homicides and missing persons.

Consider a recent example of Flock in action. In August, after five people were killed on a rural property outside Forest Grove, Ore., the suspect fled nearly 200 miles north in a pickup stolen from one of his victims. Cellphone data led investigators to believe he was in the Enumclaw, Wash., area. Enumclaw police then checked their Flock system and found multiple hits from the stolen vehicle the previous night.

Officers found the truck behind a grocery store the next afternoon, with the suspect inside, dead from an apparent suicide. A quintuple-homicide manhunt that could have lasted much longer was over in little more than a day.

Now, why would anybody be opposed to a tool that helped bring closure to a quintuple homicide case? Why have the left, right and libertarians formed common ground on this issue?

Flock critics have conjured up scenarios in the minds of the public, labeling Flock as a gateway to a 1984-type totalitarian state, in which every citizen could be made to conform to a strict government-approved way of life. Any form of disobedience detected by Flock hardware could be stamped out and all noncompliance swiftly met with prison time or worse. Governments could make religion illegal, and Flock could be used to track down peaceful worshipers. Governments might outlaw specific groups, and surveillance technology could be used to track them.

A government official could misuse the information for personal purposes. An obsessive ex-lover could use someone’s movements to track them down . Flock could make such abuses easier to perpetrate. But this is where Flock critics commit a dangerous logical fallacy: the package deal.

A package deal treats two separate ideas as though they were one: “Flock recorded this information” and “this information could be used in a way that harms someone.” Both are true on their own, but because the second one is alarming, the whole package gets treated as alarming, including the first part, which is simply a technological system doing what it was built to do: collect and organize information about reality.

To explain this further, the two concepts above, “Flock recorded this information” and “someone used this information to do harm,” can be synthesized into two words: “tools” and “philosophy.”

The tool — Flock cameras — can identify, classify and organize information, but they do not determine the moral purpose for which that information is used. Philosophy, on the other hand, is what guides a person’s response to reality. When an individual is presented with the facts of reality, his chosen philosophy tells him how to act on that information. A devout Catholic and an opportunistic criminal will respond differently to finding keys in a car that isn’t theirs.

With Flock, the same location data could reach a detective, a stalker or a corrupt official. The same facts produce different responses because different philosophies are doing the interpreting.

If an obsessive ex-lover uses Flock to locate someone they intend to stalk, the wrongdoing is not contained in the fact that the person’s location was recorded. The wrongdoing occurs when a person takes that information and uses it for an immoral end.

On that note, Flock’s auditing system can help expose precisely that kind of misuse. Its logs record what happens in the database , just as its cameras record what happens on the roads. When an officer improperly searches for someone’s movements, that action leaves a record that can be reviewed and exposed.

A critic might respond that this misses the point. Flock does not merely record information; it makes that information far easier to collect, search and use. Flock increases the scale, speed and accessibility of information that was previously scattered across thousands of individual observations, which increases the potential for misuse. But the power of a tool does not determine the morality of the end it serves. Again, the package deal confuses the tool with the philosophy of the person directing its application.

A car makes it easier to travel. A telephone makes it easier to communicate. A computer makes it easier to process information. A Flock camera makes it easier to catch criminals. Each of these technologies makes it easier for an individual to accomplish something, and consequently easier for that individual to misuse it.

If making wrongdoing easier were sufficient reason to eliminate a technology, we would eventually have to reject all technology per se. A criminal can use a car to flee a crime scene. A stalker can use a telephone to harass someone. A thief can use a computer to steal information. But the existence of these possibilities does not make the car, telephone or computer immoral. The answer is not technological regression — it is to hold individuals who deliberately misuse the technology responsible for what they do.

If a government is committed to violating the rights of its citizens, it will seek the means to do so, with or without Flock. Cutting down Flock cameras does not eliminate the government’s or any individual’s rotten philosophy that could lead to a rights violation. A tool in the hands of individuals with a rights-respecting philosophy will solve crimes and, consequently, protect the rights of the people. We can live in a world where stolen cars, kidnapped persons and violent criminals can be found in mere minutes, rather than months or not at all.

The choice before every person weighing Flock is not surveillance versus liberty. It is whether a free people answers evil by punishing evildoers or by cutting out its own eyes.

Kevin Babicz is an entrepreneur and founder of Young Capitalists for the World.
