articles.title: Newsom says he’s a ‘disrupter at heart’
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) cast himself as a political “disrupter” in an interview published this week, as the Democratic state leader publicly weighs a presidential bid in 2028. In a series of interviews with Vanity Fair published Wednesday, Newsom discussed the recent surge of support for democratic socialist candidates this midterm cycle and pushed…
articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) cast himself as a political “disrupter” in an interview published this week, as the Democratic state leader publicly weighs a presidential bid in 2028.

In a series of interviews with Vanity Fair published Wednesday, Newsom discussed the recent surge of support for democratic socialist candidates this midterm cycle and pushed back against the idea that he was a part of the Democratic Party’s establishment.

“I’m not,” he told Vanity Fair’s Joe Hagan. “I mean, I’ve been at this awhile. To the extent I’m established, in that context — but I’m notoriously a disrupter at heart. I’ve never been for the status quo, and I tend to take risks to a degree that few elected officials do.”

Several Democratic lawmakers running this election cycle have similarly sought to position themselves as political outsiders amid Democratic voters’ embrace of a wave of new candidates affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

Newsom criticized the DSA as trading in “slogans” in an interview with Vanity Fair.

“So much of what DSA is promoting, I’m like, ‘Been there, done that,’” he said, referencing legislation he signed into law limiting annual rent increases and placing new restrictions on evictions in California.

The governor said he is also “the biggest climate champion that you know,” but he added, “I’m not antibusiness.”

Additionally, Hagan pressed Newsom about his recent comment to CNN that he would not run for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris enters the race, arguing they would be competing for the same supporter base.

“You can’t hold off on making a decision, waiting, waiting, waiting,” he told Hagan. “But I don’t think that will — I’m not concerned about that, candidly.”

The governor also addressed rising concerns among the American public with advanced artificial technology development — a major industry in his state. If elected president, Newsom said he would lead “an international movement focusing on the issue of truth and safety and trust.”

He expressed concern that some leaders in the industry have been changed by access to power, saying he’s “lost relationships with these guys.” Newsom did not specify which tech executives he was referencing.

“What the hell happened to these people? I have animus now that I never had,” Newsom told Vanity Fair.

“I think power corrupts — how they’ve been able to corrupt and manipulate the political system,” he continued. “I don’t care if they voted for [President] Trump. They were always libertarian. But it’s the nature of just too much abundance, too much wealth, too much isolation, too much indulgence, and too much power. Because the money buys you power.”

The governor also touted draft pages of a “Project 2029” policy framework for Democrats — an apparent reference to MAGA’s “ Project 2025 ” proposal for the second Trump administration.

Newsom said he has about “eight pages of commonsense good policy ideas” included in the draft framework.

“This is just policy, not narrative, the kinds of things we need to do: zoning reform, corporate tax, junk-fee stuff, new domestic strategies and tariffs, preschool things, a cap on childcare, family leave, paid sick leave, child tax credits, industrial decarbonization, anti-monopoly stuff, immigration, whistleblower protections,” Newsom said.

Newsom expressed optimism about his ability to hold his own in what could be a competitive Democratic presidential primary.

“I don’t have a problem fighting. Nor do I have a problem getting roughed up and getting back up,” he told Vanity Fair. “I’ve been road tested. It’s not small ball out here in California.”

articles.title: DOJ seeks to censure judges who spoke to the Times about Minnesota immigration raids
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Wednesday took the remarkable step of seeking to censure both a former and sitting federal judge in Minnesota after the pair spoke to The New York Times about the Trump administration’s immigration surge in the state. The two judges are Patrick Schiltz, an appointee of former President George W.…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Wednesday took the remarkable step of seeking to censure both a former and sitting federal judge in Minnesota after the pair spoke to The New York Times about the Trump administration’s immigration surge in the state.

The two judges are Patrick Schiltz, an appointee of former President George W. Bush, and John Tunheim, an appointee of former President Clinton.

The complaint also asked the Judicial Council of the 8th Circuit to initiate an investigation into other “anonymous” judges who spoke to the outlet.

The reference is confusing, as the article named several judges on the bench who spoke to the Times on the record, including an appointee of President Trump. However, many of their comments did not directly touch on cases.

One of those comments, from Trump-appointed Judge Nancy Brasel, noted judges “are allowed to speak out about judicial independence.”

The story noted that judges were critical of how the Trump administration operated as it conducted immigration raids across the Twin Cities. Two U.S. citizens were killed during interactions with immigration agents, and the aggressive enforcement prompted bipartisan criticism, leading the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to shift to quieter tactics.

Schiltz previously noted that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) had defied 96 orders from 74 judges.

The DOJ argued in the filing that the two judges “have flagrantly violated the Code of Judicial Conduct with their improper and unethical comments.”

“Judges are ethically prohibited from commenting publicly on cases pending in any court and making political or policy statements concerning matters that are or have been before them,” the DOJ wrote, adding that the “canon” applies to media interviews.

“These judges should be ordered to recuse from any matters involving DHS because the public reasonably questions their impartiality in cases involving immigration. Moreover, the Eighth Circuit should initiate an investigation by the Judicial Counsel into the improper conduct by judges in the District of Minnesota who ‘covet publicity’ rather than adhering to the rule of law by adjudicating cases or controversies.”

A spokesperson for the U.S. District Court in Minnesota said judges were well within the bounds of ethics guidelines.

“As legal-ethics experts have confirmed, our judges were acting well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges in speaking to the New York Times. Indeed, in February of this year, the Committee on Codes of Conduct issued an advisory opinion to emphasize that federal judges may ‘speak[] and writ[e] on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence.’ Our judges acted within this capacity,” spokesperson Rebeccah Parks stated in an email.

Schlitz told the Times that on court orders “most, if not all, of the noncompliance was due to incompetence” and also said that level of defiance “just never happens.”

Tunheim also made brief remarks to the Times, saying that the widespread arrests did not focus on those with a criminal record.

“They weren’t arresting, in my view, people who were dangerous criminals on the street,” said Tunheim.

The DOJ argued that Tunheim’s remarks “while less verbose” were “equally unethical.”

“Opining that the Administration was not arresting illegal aliens who were ‘dangerous criminals’ is factually inaccurate and unvarnished political commentary,” the DOJ wrote.

Legal boards that govern the judiciary in recent years have affirmed the ability of judges to make some public comments.

An advisory opinion from the Judicial Conference’s Committee on Codes of Conduct affirms that the ethics code abided by judges allows them to advocate for the rule of law and defend the independence of the courts, including to seek increased judicial security and funding.

The opinion goes further to say that, in some circumstances, judges may stand up for their peers against unjust attacks.

“Although this Commentary addresses persecution specifically, the Committee believes the Code and its previous advisory opinions leave room, in at least some circumstances, for the measured defense of judicial colleagues from illegitimate forms of criticism and attacks that risk undermining judicial independence or the rule of law, whether or not they rise to the level of persecution,” the opinion states.

articles.title: Blanche announces charges against 10 permanent residents accused of Minnesota voter fraud
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche announced indictments of 10 lawful permanent residents accused of noncitizen voting in Minnesota elections since 2022.
articles.body: Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Wednesday that a federal grand jury had indicted ten lawful permanent residents accused of voting illegally or attempting to do so in multiple Minnesota elections, including the state’s August 2026 primary. The ten defendants, originally from Liberia, Canada, South Africa, Brazil, Bosnia, Germany, Ghana and Lithuania, allegedly lied to election officials and told them they were U.S. citizens so they could register to vote. They were accused of voting in the 2022 and 2024 general elections, according to court records. "Voter fraud erodes the public's trust in our electoral system, and it's vital to our democratic process that we do everything that we can to restore that trust," Blanche said at a news conference announcing the charges. FEDERAL INDICTMENT HANDED DOWN IN MINNESOTA RELATED TO ISSUE SOME DEMS CLAIM NEVER HAPPENS: 'HOTBED FOR FRAUD' "The most basic way the Department of Justice can accomplish this restoration of trust is by working to make sure the only people voting in an election in the United States are American citizens who are eligible to vote." The 10 defendants were charged separately. They are Bhator Konah Bryant, 61, of Liberia; Edvile Vaidoto Edmunds, 59, of Lithuania; Joshua Frederick Kofi Edzie, 63, of Ghana; Alan Barbu Kargbo, 48, of Liberia; Paul Kras, 78, of Germany; Fadil Rasim Ozegovic, 58, of Bosnia; Aparecido Donizetti Padovan, 62, of Brazil; Chris Adam Pettiquoi, 43, of Liberia; Christian Liam Schenk, 47, of Canada; and Hester Sophia Weihmann, 69, of South Africa. Bryant appears to be the only defendant who wasn't charged with voting illegally, only falsely claiming citizenship in 2024 to register. Making a false citizenship claim to vote is a felony punishable by up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, while voting by a noncitizen is a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in prison and a $100,000 fine. Blanche also expressed frustration that the media has, in his view, not taken the Justice Department's work prosecuting election fraud cases seriously to this point. BIDEN ADMINISTRATION GRANTED WOMAN GREEN CARD MONTHS BEFORE SHE ILLEGALLY VOTED IN 2024 ELECTION: DHS "I don't know what the number is that will work for you guys. Whether it's 106, maybe it's 120," he said, referring to a hypothetical number of investigations. "At some point, it has to become meaningful to to the media." Blanche said since President Donald Trump has returned to office, the Justice Department has charged more than 90 people with voter fraud offenses, including 50 illegal immigrants in the past five weeks. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there have been 10 voter fraud-related convictions and that there are more than 1,600 active investigations into similar conduct across the country. Mullin did not answer a reporter’s question about how the department plans to use the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements database, known as SAVE, to identify voters who may be ineligible ahead of the midterms. STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS The Supreme Court ruled Friday that the administration may use the database for voter-eligibility checks while litigation continues. SAVE has historically been used to help government agencies verify whether noncitizens applying for public benefits are eligible to receive them. States’ use of the SAVE database is voluntary, but federal law generally bars states from conducting systematic voter-roll purges within 90 days of a federal election. With the midterms less than a month away, the Supreme Court’s ruling is expected to have limited immediate impact. During the same news conference Wednesday, Blanche also announced that the Justice Department had filed a judicial misconduct complaint with the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals against several Minnesota federal judges who spoke with The New York Times about cases the department said were still pending. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The article, published Sept. 17, centered on an interview with Judge Patrick J. Schiltz, who said Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) violated nearly 100 orders from the federal district court in Minnesota during the height of Operation Metro Surge, which saw hundreds of federal agents in the streets of Minneapolis throughout January of this year. Schiltz, a George W. Bush appointee, told the Times that the alleged violation of these orders likely came down to incompetence and staffing shortages at the Justice Department. Blanche said Schiltz airing various complaints about the Trump administration to the Times was a violation of judicial canons and his ethical duties. "We have asked the 8th Circuit to conduct an investigation, and in the meantime, we ask that these judges recuse themselves from every case involving DHS, either criminal or civil in nature, because of the obvious bias they have shown in this article," Blanche said. Shiltz issued this response to Fox News, "As legal ethics experts have confirmed, I was acting well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges in speaking to The New York Times. Indeed, in February of this year, the Committee on Codes of Conduct issued an advisory opinion to emphasize that federal judges may ‘speak[] and writ[e] on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence.’ That is exactly what I did."

articles.title: 'Drug-dealing' network shielded by blue states targeted in SCOTUS challenge
articles.summary: Louisiana Republican Attorney General Liz Murrill filed two lawsuits targeting blue-state shield laws and the online abortion pill pipeline.
articles.body: Louisiana Republican Attorney General Liz Murrill is escalating her fight against abortion pills entering states that ban abortions through two lawsuits — one targeting the providers accused of distributing the drugs and another challenging the blue-state laws shielding them from prosecution. Murrill, along with Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall and Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin, sued New York, California and Massachusetts at the Supreme Court on Wednesday, alleging their shield laws block cooperation with investigations into abortion-pill providers. The attorneys general also filed a separate lawsuit in Louisiana against more than 30 people and organizations accused of advertising, prescribing, dispensing or shipping abortion pills into their states. "This is drug dealing and it's illegal," Murrill told Fox News Digital. "And we're going to continue to do everything that we can to enforce the laws in our states." The two lawsuits, filed Wednesday, are the latest move in a widening state-by-state fight over abortion. That conflict has grown since the Supreme Court's 2022 ruling in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, which struck down Roe v. Wade and gave elected officials the power to set abortion policy in their states. HAWLEY SENDS CRIMINAL REFERRAL OF 'LEFT-WING DARK-MONEY' GROUP OVER MAILED ABORTION DRUGS Murrill said the Supreme Court case targets the blue states' legal protections that have thwarted Louisiana's previous efforts to prosecute out-of-state doctors. "These shield laws are very comprehensive," Murrill said, arguing that California and New York prohibit officials from assisting other states seeking to enforce judgments stemming from abortion-related conduct. Louisiana has already indicted New York physician Margaret Carpenter and California physician Remy Coeytaux over allegations that they prescribed abortion drugs that were sent into Louisiana. New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul and California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom have refused to extradite the doctors. The Supreme Court complaint cited Louisiana's unsuccessful effort to extradite Carpenter, saying Hochul declared there was "no way in hell" she would comply with Louisiana's request. The filing said New York later strengthened its shield law, including by allowing prescribers of abortion drugs to keep their names off prescription labels. Newsom similarly rejected Louisiana's request to extradite Coeytaux in January, saying California would not help other states punish doctors for providing abortion access that is legal in California. CALIFORNIA ABORTION PILL SUPPLIERS PLOT WORKAROUNDS AHEAD OF SUPREME COURT MIFEPRISTONE DECISION When Murrill vowed to sue, Newsom responded on X telling her to "Go f--- yourself. California will never help you criminalize healthcare." "I think that if I sent guns into their states illegally, they would certainly try to come after me," Murrill told Fox News Digital. "I said specifically at the time that we would be coming for them and we are." "We are going to take down those laws using every tool that we have at our disposal," she continued. The second lawsuit directly targets what Murrill calls the "pill pipeline." The 100-page complaint alleges providers used online questionnaires to obtain information from customers before abortion drugs were mailed into states where their distribution is prohibited. The states allege some organizations openly acknowledged that their conduct violated those states' laws while relying on shield laws to protect themselves from legal consequences. Murrill said investigators have conducted controlled purchases and received pills packaged in small bags, sometimes in quantities she said exceeded what would ordinarily be prescribed. "We've seen it for ourselves," Murrill said. "There's no supervision, there's no healthcare, there's no communication whatsoever. It's all done online." Murrill argued that the system can allow people other than pregnant women to obtain the drugs, pointing to cases Louisiana authorities said involved women being pressured or deceived into taking abortion medication. PRO-LIFE LEADER SOUNDS ALARM AFTER DOCTOR GETS 6 MONTHS FOR FORCING ABORTION PILLS ON GIRLFRIEND "We have a situation in one town in Louisiana that we've documented and investigated where a father did not want his teenage daughter to keep a pregnancy," Murrill told Fox News Digital. "And so he basically put the medication in a smoothie, forced her to drink it. She did ultimately give birth to that baby at 23 weeks and is still in a NICU fighting for its life." The attorney general also said Louisiana wants more help from the Trump administration. "Obviously we think the FDA could be doing more and we've asked them to do that," Murrill said. Louisiana has separately challenged federal rules that eliminated an in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone. Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America President Marjorie Dannenfelser backed the litigation, accusing blue states of using their laws "to obstruct justice" and urging the Justice Department to settle Louisiana's separate FDA litigation. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "Democrats’ pro-abortion extremism has brought this country to a crisis point. Abortion activists flagrantly sell dangerous drugs across state lines and women and children pay the price, with more and more survivors of ‘death in a pill’ bravely coming forward," Dannenfelser said in a statement. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to New York, California and Massachusetts' governors' offices for comment.

articles.title: Lara Trump says Iran war could cost Trump the midterms
articles.summary: President Trump’s daughter-in-law Lara Trump said Tuesday the Iran war could cost him the midterm elections but insisted that losing both chambers of Congress would be worth the cost. British journalist Harry Cole spoke with Lara Trump, also a former Republican National Committee co-chair, on his YouTube show “Harry Cole Saves the West.” He asked…
articles.body:
President Trump’s daughter-in-law Lara Trump said Tuesday the Iran war could cost him the midterm elections but insisted that losing both chambers of Congress would be worth the cost.

British journalist Harry Cole spoke with Lara Trump, also a former Republican National Committee co-chair, on his YouTube show “ Harry Cole Saves the West .” He asked about her outlook on the midterms while the Iranians are “dragging their feet on doing any form of deal.” Cole said the conflict “could cost him [Trump] his legacy.”

“Well, it could cost him these midterms,” she replied. “I think Donald Trump’s legacy has yet to be written and I think that, in a lot of ways, maybe — I still say he’s going to go down in history as one of the greatest presidents — if not, the greatest America has ever seen.”

She later said the president “really hates the way that things have gone with Iran” and wished that “things had more swiftly happened.”

“But you’re right, the Iranians are absolutely holding out until these midterm elections,” Lara Trump continued. “They want to do everything they can to damage this president’s hopes of these midterms going his way because they think it’s going to give them an advantage.”

These comments are at odds with what Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told reporters at the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly last week.

“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Pezeshkian said, responding to President Trump’s earlier claim that the regime is waiting until after Americans hit the polls to settle the conflict.

Cole later pressed Lara Trump on the administration’s case for the war and whether it would be worth losing both chambers in November to the Democrats.

“Yeah,” she answered. “Look, I think he just understands that when Iran gets a nuclear weapon, it doesn’t matter who is in charge of the House. It doesn’t matter the majority in the Senate. This world is a really frightening place and you really can’t come back from that.”

She defended the president’s accomplishments in the Middle East despite dealing with the “lunatics” in Iran.

Cole said he views the conflict as one that the administration has not made a “complete case for” and asked if enough has been done to explain to Americans why the conflict is happening as gas prices soar.

Lara Trump said Americans feel “far removed” from Iran geographically and that her father-in-law “talks about it a lot.”

“But I think it would be beneficial to hear from other Republicans, from other folks at the White House, from other people out there in this space, more about exactly what was on the line and how close I think we were to the world being a very different and very scary place if Iran ever actually developed a nuclear weapon,” she said.

The U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran reached the seven-month mark Monday, a military operation that the president said would be an “excursion” that would conclude on a short timeline .

Republican lawmakers have largely supported his decision to launch strikes, but some with their eyes toward winning races in November have called for a quick end to the conflict to allow gas prices to moderate.

Iran closed off the Strait of Hormuz after the initial strikes in February, effectively cutting off roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil from being exported globally through the strait. He has defended the higher prices as a “ very inexpensive price to pay ” to stop Iran’s nuclear ambitions.

articles.title: Trump says US exit from Iraq a ‘victory’ for both countries
articles.summary: President Trump touted the final withdrawal of U.S. troops from Iraq as a win for both countries more than 20 years after the start of the Iraq War. “It’s a victory for the United States, it’s a victory for Iraq and a decisive victory over ISIS, which has been completely decimated,” Trump said speaking at…
articles.body:
President Trump touted the final withdrawal of U.S. troops from Iraq as a win for both countries more than 20 years after the start of the Iraq War.

“It’s a victory for the United States, it’s a victory for Iraq and a decisive victory over ISIS, which has been completely decimated,” Trump said speaking at a Hispanic Heritage Month event at the White House on Wednesday.

Trump’s comments echoed those he made in a Truth Social post prior to the event.

“I had a choice to stay or to leave, and felt, without question, that it was time for America to go home!” the president wrote.

He also voiced his support for Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who was elected to his post in May. Al-Zaidi met with Trump at the White House in July.

Trump’s comments come after U.S. Central Command (Centcom) announced the departure of U.S. forces from Iraq, marking an end to its 12-year military mission.

Centcom said that all U.S. forces and military equipment left Erbil Air Base in the northern part of the country and that a “transition “to a U.S.-Iraq bilateral defense relationship” would begin.

Centcom head Adm. Brad Cooper said in a statement that “full primary responsibility for Iraq’s security to the government and Iraq and the brave people of Iraq,” while U.S. troops in the region will maintain “vigilance and readiness” in “protecting the U.S. homeland and strengthening regional security.”

The U.S. invaded Iraq in 2003, toppling dictator Saddam Hussein. The war went on for years after former President George W. Bush, who led the U.S. effort without a formal declaration of war, departed the White House.

articles.title: Here are the Republicans backing Democratic candidates in the midterms
articles.summary: A number of Republicans have come out in support of Democratic candidates ahead of the November elections, as control of both chambers of Congress is up for grabs. A former governor, a GOP election official and a former Senate candidate are among the small but growing list of Republicans who have crossed the aisle to…
articles.body:
A number of Republicans have come out in support of Democratic candidates ahead of the November elections, as control of both chambers of Congress is up for grabs.

A former governor, a GOP election official and a former Senate candidate are among the small but growing list of Republicans who have crossed the aisle to endorse their party’s opposition. Some Republicans who won’t go as far as to endorse the Democrats are voicing frustration and sometimes opposition to GOP candidates.

There is at least one high-profile example of a Democrat backing a Republican: Outgoing Democratic Rep. Jared Golden (Maine) is supporting Rep. Mike Lawler (N.Y.) in his reelection fight .

But in general, there are more examples of Republicans backing Democrats this cycle a,id President Trump’s sinking approval ratings. Democrats are widely expected to win back the House majority and are now seen as having a chance to win the Senate majority.

Graves endorsed Democrat Adam Hamilton over Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) earlier this month.

Hamilton, a popular Methodist minister, is running to unseat Marshall in a race that has been viewed as increasingly competitive in recent months.

Graves served from 1995 until 2003, making him the state’s longest-serving GOP governor. He announced his endorsement in a video posted to the social media platform X earlier this month.

“For the last six years, Sen. Roger Marshall has turned his back on Kansas,” Graves said, adding that Hamilton “stands as a bulwark of kindness” and service to others.

Graves has endorsed Democrats before. In 2018 and 2022 , he backed Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly (D) over her GOP opponents, with Kelly winning both times .

Georgia Peanut Commission Chair Donald Chase

The Republican chair of the Georgia Peanut Commission, Donald Chase, endorsed Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) for reelection earlier this week.

“We don’t necessarily elect a party,” Chase told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution . “I like to support people that I can get behind and believe in.”

A few other Republicans have also lined up behind Ossoff, including Julie Smith and Scott James Matheson — the GOP mayors of Tifton, Ga., and Valdosta, Ga., respectively.

Flake, who has been outspoken against Trump for years, has also endorsed Ossoff.

Flake condemned Trump’s refusal to concede in the 2020 election as “awful for the country.” He spoke out against the president’s attacks on the press during his first term and endorsed former Vice President Kamala Harris for president in 2024.

Ossoff is facing Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.) in a race that forecasters predict will go in Democrats’ favor.

South Dakota Secretary of State Monae Johnson

Johnson, who is leaving her office, backed Democrat Terrence Davis in the race to succeed her after losing the GOP nomination to a primary challenger in June.

Johnson encouraged voters to look beyond a candidate’s party and said Davis is best prepared for the job.

“He has publicly identified transparency, voting rights and making government systems work for the people who use them as priorities of his candidacy,” Johnson said. “Those areas have a direct connection to the work of the secretary of state’s office.”

In the Kansas Senate race, Naramore — a Republican who challenged Marshall in the primary — also announced his support for Hamilton in a video last week .

Naramore said he still identifies as a Republican but criticized Marshall for his support of Trump’s tariffs and his questioned residency in the state of Kansas.

“Adam Hamilton’s family has been in Kansas for five generations,” Naramore said. “He spent more than 40 years as a pastor, not a politician. He will fight for all of us: Republicans, Democrats and Independents.”

articles.title: US Fed watchdog finds no criminal wrongdoing in Powell-era renovation costs
articles.summary: The renovation costs became a focus of Trump’s pressure campaign against former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell.
articles.body:
The Federal Reserve’s inspector general has found no grounds for a criminal referral or evidence of administrative misconduct tied to a costly United States central bank renovation project that became a focal point of President Donald Trump’s pressure campaign against former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell.

The watchdog released its findings on Wednesday after reviewing the renovation of two venerable Fed buildings in Washington, DC. The project has run roughly $1bn over budget, bringing its estimated cost to about $2.4bn.

“At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the US attorney general,” the inspector general said.

Trump repeatedly used the renovation costs to attack Powell during his time as Fed chief. The president had consistently pressured Powell to lower interest rates.

A US Department of Justice investigation into the project and Powell’s congressional testimony was closed earlier this year after a federal judge agreed with Powell that they were a pretext for pressuring the Fed chief to lower interest rates.

This most recent watchdog report has identified significant shortcomings in the Fed’s management of the project, including its failure to establish an intended “guaranteed maximum price” that would have shifted responsibility for cost overruns to the contractor.

It also found that design features criticised by the White House, including marble, water features and a garden terrace, “did not materially contribute” to the overruns.

Cost overruns on government projects are common, with Trump’s budget for White House ballroom construction having doubled from initial estimates.

articles.title: US FCC head says controversial Trump ads do not raise concerns
articles.summary: Series of publicly-funded television spots have been criticised by Republicans and Democrats as self-promotion by Trump.
articles.body:
A series of taxpayer-funded advertisements that critics say are political campaign spots for United States President Donald Trump are not improper and do not need to be reviewed, according to the head of the country’s broadcast regulator.

“There’s nothing in there that strikes me to merit any sort of FCC review,” Brendan Carr, who Trump appointed as head of the Federal Communications Commission, said on Wednesday.

Carr likened the advertisements to public service announcements, echoing an argument the White House has made in response to criticism that Trump was using public funding to promote himself and his policies. Media freedom groups have criticised Carr for helping Trump to “weaponise” the FCC to go after news and television networks whose coverage of him he has not been happy with.

The US Constitution bars Trump from running for a third term as president, but he has nevertheless floated a third stint in the White House and has promoted merchandise bearing the words “Trump 2028”.

“The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads,” the White House said in a statement last week defending the campaign. “President Trump is not on the ballot, and there is no call to action. Instead, the announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending — at home, at the border, and abroad.”

On Tuesday, Democratic senators wrote to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) asking it to stop spending funds on a series of television advertisements promoting the Trump administration’s recent actions.

“These ads need to immediately come off the air, taxpayers need to be paid back for this theft, and everyone responsible needs to be held accountable for this corrupt and illegal propaganda,” Senators Patty Murray and Chris Murphy wrote in a letter to the agency’s head. The lawmakers said DHS was planning to spend $20m on the advertisements.

But criticism of the television spots has come from prominent Democrats as well as Republican lawmakers, who have said the campaign appears to violate legal provisions meant to bar publicly funded political propaganda.

Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, said the advertisements resembled something former Hungarian leader Viktor Orban would put out.

Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota said he agreed with the message in one of the advertisements, but “it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars”.

Some Democrats have been more direct, saying the administration could face criminal liability for its actions. “This may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes,” Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, wrote on X, citing a Trump advertisement that aired recently.

Raskin said any government employees who worked on it could have violated the Hatch Act, a 1939 law that specifically prohibits government employees from engaging in political activities.

The advertisements have aired on national television during national sports matches and other highly-watched programming.

One advertisement is a monochrome video featuring Trump walking down a hall in slow motion. In an audio clip taken from his last presidential election campaign, Trump can be heard saying Americans are now engaged in a “final battle” and that he and his supporters will “demolish the deep state, expel the warmongers from our government, we will drive out the globalists, we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists”.

In another advertisement, a montage of Trump is shown with audio of him saying, “Together, we will defeat communism, socialism, and Marxism,” before text in red capital letters notes a series of claimed accomplishments like “largest tax cuts in American history” and “reigniting American manufacturing”.

The advertisement is set to a song titled Love Me by artist JMSN, who wrote last week on X that Trump had used it without permission. Lawyers representing the artist wrote to the White House on Monday, saying they would take further action if the music was not removed from the video. JMSN, the letter said “does not want to be viewed as directly or indirectly affiliated with the President or his Administration.”

articles.title: Trump says ‘MAGA and REAL Patriots’ will never like Fox News over hosting Democrats
articles.summary: President Trump on Wednesday went after Fox News over hosting Democrats on their network, with the president saying “MAGA, and REAL Patriots will never like Fox!” “Why does FoxNews always put Chuck Schumer, Hakeem Jeffries, Jessica Tarlov, and every Democrat on, saying bad things about the Republican Party and, of course, me?” the president said…
articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday went after Fox News over hosting Democrats on their network, with the president saying “MAGA, and REAL Patriots will never like Fox!”

“Why does FoxNews always put Chuck Schumer, Hakeem Jeffries, Jessica Tarlov, and every Democrat on, saying bad things about the Republican Party and, of course, me?” the president said in a Wednesday afternoon Truth Social post.

“I actually think they get more airtime than Pro Republicans. This is why MAGA, and REAL Patriots, will never like Fox! They repeat a completely negative narrative, on and on it goes, and then we get a quick retort. It’s truly amazing that I won all three Elections,” he added, repeating his false claim that he won the 2020 presidential election.

Trump has a long history of attacking the media and press outlets, but Fox News has a history of praise from the president and he has also hired former Fox News personalities into his administration.

Last month, Trump went after “Fox News Sunday” anchor Shannon Bream because of on-air guests, charts and polls he claimed did not show off successful actions by his administration.

“In any event, Shannon’s ‘show’ is beyond redemption. Fortunately, MAGA, which is close to 100% of the Republican Party, understands that, and watch her ‘Ratings’ start to fall,” Trump said on Truth Social at the time.

“Chris Wallace was bad, but Shannon is even worse,” he added, referring to her predecessor.

Fox News was also one of the major TV networks that rotate covering the president for wider media distribution that recently said they would not do so after Trump barred three media outlets from the White House earlier this month.

The Hill has reached out to Fox News for comment.

He defended a 20 percent cut to slots slated for admirals and generals as part of his push to overhaul the outlook of the Defense Department, calling it the “bare minimum” and said…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is delivering his “State of the Force” address to a select group of service members at Quantico, Va. He defended a 20 percent cut to slots slated for admirals and generals as part of his push to overhaul the outlook of the Defense Department, calling it the “bare minimum” and said it is overdue.

The Senate on Wednesday is putting lawmakers on record on bills that ban new stock trades by lawmakers and address the growth of data centers.

It’s part of an effort by Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) to throw a political lifeline to embattled Republican incumbent Sens. Jon Husted (Ohio), Pete Ricketts (Neb.) and Dan Sullivan (Alaska).

Senate Democrats blocked Ricketts’s Stop Insider Trading Act, taking it down by a 53-47 vote. And Democrats did not provide the Ratepayer Protection Act with the 60 votes needed to overcome the filibuster, blocking it in a procedural vote, 57-43, with four Democrats joining Republicans.

The U.S. Court of International Trade is set to hear arguments in a lawsuit by a group of small businesses against President Trump, attempting to reverse his latest round of tariffs.

Trump placed the import taxes on more than 60 trading partners in July. But rather than pointing to an emergency statute to argue in favor of the tariffs — a defense that failed in the Supreme Court — the administration is now defending them under the Trade Act of 1974. Oral arguments will begin in New York City at 10 a.m. EDT. The president will not appear in court.

Trump will host a Hispanic Heritage Month celebration at 1 p.m. and then make an announcement alongside Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Meanwhile, the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee will hold a hearing on AI agents going rogue at 2:30 p.m. It comes days after OpenAI confirmed reports that its technology accessed government websites — including the Department of Education — without authorization.
